entry.title: Enterprise Management Layer EML, Model Company or Pick your own SAP Best Practices. Which to choose?
entry.content:
Enterprise Management Layer, Model Company or Pick your own SAP Best Practices. Which to choose ?

Three acceleration options built on the same foundation — and how to pick the right one (or combine all three).

 

Figure 1 — Enterprise Management Layer, Model Company and SAP Best Practices: three options built on SAP S/4HANA integrated processes, complementary and combinable.

One question. Three answers.

Every SAP S/4HANA transformation starts with the same decision: where do we begin?

Should you use:

  • Production Ready multinational preconfigured foundation that is built by SAP for your use case, addressing your Group, Tax & Localization requirements along with a setup which is tailored for you?
  • Leverage SAP's industry expertise through an executable reference solution that accelerates Fit-to-Standard and supports informed transformation decisions?
  • Or adopt proven standard business processes and configurations with the flexibility to select and activate the scope your organization needs?

Enterprise Management Layer, Model Company and SAP Best Practices each answer this question differently. They are not competing products — they are all built on the same foundation — but they solve different problems, serve different customer profiles and come with very different delivery models.

Getting the choice wrong costs time. Getting it right — or knowing when to combine them — can take weeks off your Fit-to-Standard timeline before your first workshop even starts.

1. Enterprise Management Layer for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition: Production Ready Template for Multinational Organisations

For multinational organisations, the challenge in an S/4HANA transformation goes beyond validating standard processes. The system must support a consistent corporate operating model across different countries, legal entities, accounting principles and statutory obligations — all at once. This is a requirement even before Fit-to-standard workshops can begin.

Enterprise Management Layer is built for exactly that scenario. It delivers a preconfigured SAP S/4HANA multinational foundation, built by SAP for every customer, ready to deploy into your Development, Quality and Production landscape from the moment it is handed over. Business users can begin Fit-to-Standard validation on Day 1 once their Fit-to-Standard system is created — not after weeks of baseline setup.

The scope of what Enterprise Management Layer delivers out of the box is significant:

  • Up to 49 countries (43 SAP Best Practices countries + 6 Finance-led), localised and pre-activated
  • 25 system languages pre-installed, including Arabic, Chinese, Japanese and more
  • Three-ledger parallel accounting — Group GAAP, Local GAAP and Tax ledgers — configured and ready
  • Up to 220+ standard scope items active from Day 1
  • Additional Localisations for countries which are not yet available in Standard Best Practices.
  • Customer specific configuration such as 7 Service Options (VP01–VP07) covering intercompany, engineering, service processes and more — at no additional licence cost
  • Business process documentation, test scripts, configuration documents, how-to guides and process flow diagrams, all aligned to the delivered setup
  • Built by SAP to give you the peace of mind that the system will work as its designed by Experts for your individual needs.

Built by SAP, tailored to your configuration to enable your transformation decisions

Enterprise Management Layer is not a one-size-fits-all template. Every delivery starts with a customer questionnaire that captures the agreed configuration. The decisions made there directly shape the system SAP builds and delivers. Some of the details in the questionnaire are:

  • Country coverage — which countries and local requirements must be supported
  • Group currency — the currency for corporate reporting alongside local currencies
  • Fiscal-year variants — the corporate calendar and local reporting periods
  • Functional scope — standard scope, optional scope and Enterprise Management Layer -specific service options (for example, intercompany HQ and trading entity configurations)
  • Ledger design — a foundation for Group, Tax and Local GAAP reporting in a global setup

SAP builds the customer-specific image in the SAP staging area, delivers it as a database backup, and the system is usable on Day 1 after restoring from backup. The customer and project team then focus on Fit-to-Standard workshops and business validation — not on baseline setup.

Production Ready: What does it mean?

Customer and partner teams identify any additional requirements/changes specific to your organization —or “deltas”—between the delivered solution and the business requirements, determining what additional configuration or changes are needed. SAP-provided artefacts are compatible with the transformation toolchain, allowing these deltas to be reflected directly in updated Business Process Diagrams.

Once the agreed deltas have been configured and validated, the solution can progress towards production using the production-ready landscape established from the database copy provided by SAP.

For organisations seeking an even more tailored setup, SAP also offers an additional SAP Landscape Transformation service, for an extra charge, to adapt organisational structures to the customer's own nomenclature. The customer provides the required mapping, and SAP applies the corresponding changes to make the delivered setup more closely aligned with the customer's organisational structure. This is an optional, separately charged SAP service and is not included in Enterprise Management Layer.

More than pre-activated Best Practices

Enterprise Management Layer is built on SAP Best Practices, but it goes further. It adds multinational accounting design, enhanced country localisation, additional intercompany and supply-chain processes, Enterprise Management Layer-specific scope items and detailed implementation documentation — all pre-tested by SAP and patched before delivery. The project team inherits a foundation that SAP has already built and validated more than 400 times since 2012.

To know more about Enterprise Management Layer see my Blog and get in Fast Lane with Enterprise Management Layer 

For a thorough reading on Enterprise Management Layer, see blog Enterprise Management Layer Information Hub

Key differentiator: Enterprise Management Layer delivers a customer-specific multinational foundation — with depth in complex accounting, localisation, production-ready configuration and full implementation documentation — so the project team can start from substance, not from Scratch. That is: A working system for your setup, where your business users can see the processes working Live in Fit-to-Standard workshops. You can make decisions which matter for your business and fast forward your transformation. "Spend your time where it will matter the most with Enterprise Management Layer". 

2. Model Company: Industry expertise translated into an executable reference solution

SAP Best Practices establishes the standard process foundation for SAP S/4HANA. Model company for SAP cloud solutions takes this further by translating SAP's industry expertise and proven business practices into a preconfigured, executable industry reference solution. By bringing together integrated end-to-end business scenarios, industry-specific configuration, representative business data and transformation assets, it provides organisations with a tangible starting point for validating industry processes, accelerating Fit-to-Standard and making informed decisions about their future operating model.

From Fit-Gap habits to Fit-to-Standard decisions

A traditional Fit-Gap discussion often begins with a catalogue of existing processes and enhancements, then asks the new system to reproduce them. A stronger Fit-to-Standard approach begins with a proven reference process and asks a different question: can the business adopt this process, and if not, what is the justified business, regulatory or competitive reason for deviating?

Model Company supports that conversation through an integrated, executable industry reference, rather than only individual scope items or abstract diagrams. Participants can work through realistic end-to-end business scenarios, evaluate whether the proven process meets the business need, and justify deviations only where necessary. This turns Fit-to-Standard into an informed design discussion and supports clean-core decisions.

Industry expertise, executable content and the transformation toolchain

Model company's particular strength lies in translating industry knowledge into a working SAP environment. Depending on the industry, line-of-business offering and release, the available content can include:

  • Industry-specific, integrated end-to-end processes and scenarios configured in an executable reference environment.
  • Industry- and line-of-business-specific configuration with representative master and transactional data, where available.
  • Process models, flows, test scripts and supporting documentation reflecting the delivered reference content.
  • Relevant transformation artifacts for SAP Signavio, SAP LeanIX and SAP Cloud ALM, were published and subject to applicable tool access and content availability.
  • An industry-informed reference baseline that helps teams validate standard processes, assess necessary deviations and prepare implementation scope.

By connecting industry knowledge, business architecture, process design and executable scenarios, Model Company helps bridge the gap between conceptual transformation objectives and practical implementation decisions. The resulting emphasis on standardisation and clean-core principles also establishes a stronger foundation for evaluating future innovation and AI use cases.

Delivery and scope considerations

Model company for SAP cloud solutions is included under applicable RISE with SAP entitlements at no additional product charge, subject to the relevant terms and conditions. Depending on the offering, customers can access Model Company through pre-activated sandbox environments or self-service activation.

Industry-specific reference content is currently localised primarily for the United States and Germany, with the flexibility to extend configurations to up to three countries upon request, subject to additional service charges.

For customers requiring a combination of multiple industries and/or lines of business within a single environment, an assemble-to-order service is available. This allows compatible model company content to be brought together according to specific business requirements, subject to technical feasibility and additional service charges.

For broader multinational transformation requirements, model company and Enterprise Management Layer (EML) can also be combined to leverage their respective industry-specific and multinational capabilities. Such combinations require an assessment of scope, release compatibility and technical dependencies and may involve additional service charges.

Model company is intended as a reference and validation environment rather than a productive customer landscape.

For more information on Model Company, please read blog by Erik Rahm: Model Company for SAP Cloud Solutions

Key differentiator: Model Company translates SAP industry expertise into a configured, executable reference solution with connected scenarios and transformation content. Its value is in accelerating industry-informed Fit-to-Standard decisions, not simply assembling or demonstrating standard scope items.

3. SAP Best Practices for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition: Pick your own

SAP Best Practices are the standard, pre-built business process configurations — covering Finance, Procurement, Sales, Manufacturing, Supply Chain and more — that underpin every S/4HANA implementation. They represent the accumulated learning from thousands of SAP implementations and are available to every S/4HANA Private Cloud customer as part of the licence.

Crucially, SAP Best Practices are also the shared foundation on which both Enterprise Management Layer and Model Company are built. They are not a lesser option — they are the layer that makes all three approaches possible.

When an organization chooses to activate SAP Best Practices directly, without Enterprise Management Layer or model company, it benefits from the flexibility to select and activate standard business processes according to its implementation requirements. The project team determines the relevant scope and manages activation and configuration using SAP's standard tooling, taking into account applicable country coverage, release-specific availability and technical dependencies. Standard test scripts are available for 43 countries, providing additional guidance and support for process validation.

The trade-off is that the team takes on the associated technical groundwork: system preparation, process activation, post-activation configuration, testing and documentation. For organisations that want that level of control — particularly for single-country, lower-complexity implementations — this is entirely appropriate.

Key differentiator: SAP Best Practices provide proven standard business processes and configuration content, enabling implementation teams to select and activate relevant scope according to their business requirements, supported countries and technical dependencies. They establish a flexible foundation for adopting SAP standards and accelerating implementation.

4. How they compare

The table below captures the key differences across the dimensions that matter most in implementation decisions. Read across the columns to see which option fits your situation — or where combining them makes sense.

 Figure 2 — Detailed comparison: Enterprise Management Layer vs Model Company vs SAP Best Practices across ten capability dimensions.

5. Better together — the case for combining them

Consider a multinational automotive manufacturer seeking to harmonise financial processes across several countries while validating industry-specific production, sales and service scenarios with business stakeholders:

  • Enterprise Management Layer (EML) provides a preconfigured multinational foundation, including organisational structures, accounting frameworks, ledger configurations, extensive country localisation and customer specific configurations build by SAP. This reduces initial configuration effort and establishes a validated baseline for multinational implementation.
  • Model company for SAP cloud solutions translates SAP's industry expertise into a preconfigured, executable industry reference solution. With integrated end-to-end business scenarios, industry-specific configuration, representative business data and supporting transformation assets, it enables stakeholders to experience proven industry practices and accelerate Fit-to-Standard validation.
  • SAP Best Practices provides the underlying standard business processes and configurations, offering flexibility to evaluate and activate additional relevant scope according to the customer's business requirements and implementation strategy.

Together, these offerings can provide a comprehensive transformation starting point, combining multinational capabilities, executable industry-specific processes and established SAP standards. By leveraging preconfigured and validated content, organisations can reduce initial setup effort, accelerate business validation and make more informed design decisions while supporting a clean-core approach.

Practical consideration: Combining these offerings requires an assessment of release compatibility, configuration dependencies, functional scope and delivery requirements. The feasibility and effort involved depend on the selected content and customer-specific circumstances; combined scenarios are not automatically validated end-to-end.

6. Which one is right for your project?

Use the profiles below as a starting guide. Most large programmes will find themselves drawn to more than one — which is exactly the point.

If your situation is…

Start with…

Complex Multinational Operations requiring parallel accounting, multi country localisation and tailored configurations – build for every Customer by SAP giving a solid production ready foundation.

Enterprise Management Layer — SAP built customer tailored foundation, prepared and tested for your requirements. Accelerate Fit-to-standard with clean core starting point and a production ready path forward.

Industry-specific exploration and early-phase validation — business stakeholders need to see realistic, connected scenarios before committing to process design

Model Company — Delivers an executable, industry-specific reference solution that accelerates Fit-to-Standard. Included under applicable RISE with SAP entitlements. For multinational transformations, Model Company and Enterprise Management Layer can be combined to leverage their respective strengths.

Standard, lower-complexity S/4HANA implementation — full control over scope selection, single-country or simple multi-country, team handles activation

SAP Best Practices — select your scope, activate with SAP tooling, build at your own pace. Available in 43 countries, included with the S/4HANA licence.

7. The goal is not to choose a winner

Enterprise Management Layer, Model Company and SAP Best Practices are not competing answers to the same question. Each solves a different problem.

Enterprise Management Layer accelerates transformation of a multinational by delivering preconfigured financial ledgers & localization for 49 countries with additional customer specific configurations such as Intercompany setup between Headquarter & Trading Company. This provides a solid fast forward start to fit-to-standard and a foundation which can be taken to production by just configuring delta (any additional requirements or changes specific to your organization you identify) on top.

Model company for SAP cloud solutions translates SAP's industry expertise into a preconfigured, executable reference solution, enabling business stakeholders, architects and implementation teams to validate proven industry processes, accelerate Fit-to-Standard and make informed design decisions based on a tangible, working baseline.

SAP Best Practices provide implementation teams with a proven foundation of standard business processes and configurations, offering the flexibility to select and activate the scope that best aligns with their business requirements and implementation strategy.

Used together, Enterprise Management Layer, Model Company for SAP cloud solutions and SAP Best Practices bring together complementary strengths in multinational capabilities, industry-specific expertise and standard business processes. This provides a comprehensive, preconfigured foundation that accelerates transformation, reduces implementation effort and supports a consistent Fit-to-Standard approach.

The real question is not which solution to choose, but how to leverage their respective strengths, individually or together, to accelerate transformation, embrace proven industry practices and establish a sustainable foundation for future innovation.

entry.title: Model company for SAP cloud solutions for Architects: From Target Architecture to an Executable Base
entry.content:
Part 2 of a blog series on model company for SAP cloud solutions

Introduction

 

Every architect knows the moment: the target architecture is documented in capability maps, process models and solution designs, but the next question is how to turn that intent into decisions the implementation team can validate and deliver.

This is my second post in the model company for SAP cloud solutions series. The first post introduced the overall proposition and the move toward Fit-to-Standard. Here, the focus is on the decisions enterprise and solution architects need to make.

Model company provides a pre-configured, executable SAP S/4HANA reference baseline with available industry and line-of-business content. It does not define every customer’s target architecture. Instead, it gives architects a working reference against which to assess capability coverage, question assumptions and identify the design decisions that remain.

Figure 1: From architectural intent to an executable reference. Model company provides a baseline for validation, not a finished customer architecture.

The Architect’s Challenge: From Design to Executable Reality

 

Target architectures describe what an organization wants to achieve; implementation teams must determine how that intent can be realized in a configured solution. The handover between the two often exposes uncertainties: Is a process already supported by standard SAP functionality? Which assumptions need testing? What requires integration, configuration or an extension?

Model company helps bridge this gap by making relevant standard processes and industry content tangible. Architects can explore and demonstrate a working reference rather than relying exclusively on diagrams or descriptions. The reference does not remove the need for discovery or customer-specific validation; it makes those activities more focused.

This supports a change in mindset, from Fit-to-Gap (“how do we reproduce what we do today?”) to Fit-to-Standard (“can the standard support the intended outcome, and where is differentiation genuinely necessary?”). The question is not whether the standard is always sufficient, but how to make deviations evidence-based architectural decisions.

Figure 2: Changing the conversation: assess business outcomes against the standard before specifying deviations.

An Architect’s Workflow: A Retail Example

 

Consider an illustrative retail transformation. The target architecture calls for improved inventory visibility, a consistent order-fulfillment process and reliable financial integration. Rather than treating every existing customization as a requirement, the architecture team can use the relevant model company reference to structure its assessment.

  • Identify the capabilities: map the target business outcomes to the processes and application responsibilities that must support them.
  • Explore the baseline: examine available retail processes and associated artifacts in the model company system. Confirm which scope and release are available.
  • Validate assumptions: demonstrate representative flows with sample data; compare the standard with key business scenarios and record the functional or non-functional questions still open.
  • Make design choices: Distinguish standard coverage from required configuration, interfaces, data work, and genuinely differentiating extensions. For each proposed deviation, document its justification, expected business value, and implications for complexity, cost, and long-term maintainability.
  • Carry decisions into delivery: use relevant process models, scope artifacts and governance tools to connect decisions to implementation requirements, testing and change control.

The result is not an automatically generated target architecture. It is a better-evidenced design: the team knows what it has validated, where uncertainty remains and which decisions require architectural ownership.

 

How It Helps Enterprise Architects

 

Enterprise architects connect strategy, business capabilities and the target operating model with the application landscape.

Model company can help them:

  • Assess capability realization in a running reference and distinguish demonstrated scope from capabilities that still require further design.
  • Relate reference business architecture and process models to the actual standard processes delivered in the relevant industry or line of business.
  • Create a shared starting point for business stakeholders, enterprise architecture and delivery teams, reducing misunderstandings about what “standard” means.
  • Inform roadmap and scoping decisions by checking current content availability, release coverage and relevant prerequisites rather than assuming that every planned capability is already delivered.

How It Helps Solution Architects

 

Solution architects translate the target into process, data, application, integration and extension decisions. Against a pre-configured reference, they can:

  • Explore representative end-to-end processes instead of starting each discussion from an unconfigured system.
  • Inspect sample master and transactional data and identify interfaces or integration requirements; a visible integration point does not necessarily mean that a connected external system has been delivered.
  • Evaluate standard functionality first, then select suitable clean-core-aligned extensibility options based on the requirement and deployment environment.
  • Use process and delivery artifacts to support documented scope, requirements and testing decisions, with traceability governed through the chosen project toolchain.

Connecting Architecture to the Delivery Toolchain

 

SAP LeanIX supports enterprise architecture and application landscape decisions; SAP Signavio provides a comprehensive process intelligence and transformation suite for process-modeling and business transformation; and SAP Cloud ALM is a full lifecycle application management platform, covering implementation governance, operations monitoring, and continuous improvement.

For transformation initiatives, it delivers end-to-end project management, structured requirements handling, and test governance, making it the central control point for managing SAP solution deployments.

Model company contributes a working reference and associated artifacts that can be used alongside these tools.

The precise artifacts available depend on the selected model company scope and release. Process models, documentation, test assets and sample data can support design and Fit-to-Standard workshops, but architects should verify what is included and how it can be accessed or imported. Viewing process content and importing or synchronizing it into a customer workspace may have different licensing and authorization requirements.

Importantly, traceability is not automatic. Connecting process models, scope, requirements and test evidence requires tool configuration, appropriate entitlements, disciplined ownership and project governance. SAP Signavio, SAP Cloud ALM synchronization, for example, has defined setup and license prerequisites.

 

Where It Fits in SAP Activate

 

Model company brings its most immediate value to early validation and Fit-to-Standard work, particularly during Explore. Its reference content and artifacts may also inform later implementation phases.

The model company system remains a reference/sandbox environment: it is not the productive customer solution and should not be described as directly deploying into production.

  • Discover and Prepare: use the available baseline to illustrate potential scope, challenge target-state assumptions and prepare more focused architectural discussions.
  • Explore (Fit-to-Standard): run relevant scenarios against the standard, assess business fit, identify genuine deltas and agree which requirements need additional design.
  • Realize: use validated decisions and applicable reference artifacts to guide implementation; govern architecture conformance, interfaces, extensions and test coverage in the customer project.
  • Deploy: confirm that the implemented productive solution meets the approved architecture, security, integration and operational criteria. This is a customer-project responsibility, not a deployment of the model company sandbox.
  • Run: maintain architectural guardrails, assess changing needs against standard capabilities, and govern extensions and process evolution over time.

The continuous thread is controlled decision-making: from intended business capability, through process validation and design, to implementation evidence. The architecture team can establish traceability across that chain but must actively maintain it.

Figure 3: Model company in SAP Activate. Explore is the primary direct validation point; later phases benefit from the reference and decisions carried forward.

Keeping the Core Clean: Extensibility Governance

 

Clean core is an architectural discipline, not a property that eliminates governance. It aims to keep the SAP core close to standard, use appropriate extension mechanisms and released interfaces, and support maintainability and future upgrades. Model company, built on SAP Best Practices that bring standard Line of Business business processes and aligned with clean-core principles, gives architects a useful starting reference, not an unconditional guarantee of customer-specific compliance or upgrade safety.

  • Challenge proposed deviations: demonstrate what standard content already covers before agreeing to custom build; record business rationale and architectural consequences for justified gaps.
  • Choose the right extension pattern: consider approved key-user, developer/on-stack and side-by-side extensibility, including SAP BTP where appropriate. The right choice depends on requirements, release and deployment model; “side-by-side” is not the answer to every extension.
  • Govern integration explicitly: design interfaces around applicable released APIs and supported integration patterns, while validating external systems, security, performance and data responsibilities.
  • Keep decisions traceable: link requirements, architectural decisions, process changes and tests within the project’s governed toolchain, rather than assuming the reference environment does this automatically.

By reducing unnecessary custom code and providing a clean-core-aligned reference, model company simplifies architectural decision-making and lifecycle management, while enabling architects to focus their assessments on customer-specific requirements, integrations, and extensions.

 

What Architects Still Need to Validate

 

A reference baseline is most useful when its boundaries are clear.

Architects must still confirm:

  • Industry and country coverage
  • Business-process fit
  • The customer’s application and integration landscape
  • Data migration and ownership
  • Non-functional requirements
  • Security and regulatory obligations
  • Extension design
  • Licensing or technical prerequisites for connected tools.

The strongest use of model company is therefore not to declare the architecture complete. It is to expose and resolve architectural questions earlier, while keeping legitimate differentiation visible and controlled.

 

From Clean Core to Validated AI Capabilities

 

Clean-core principles, standardized processes, and governed data provide a strong foundation for sustainable AI adoption. Model company for SAP cloud solutions builds on this foundation, with Joule already activated and successfully tested in selected model company environments. In addition, AI use cases have been tested and validated and are ready for inclusion, progressively extending the portfolio’s ability to demonstrate AI-enabled business processes.

For architects, this creates an opportunity to move beyond conceptual AI discussions and explore how intelligent capabilities can be incorporated into business processes and solution architectures. These validated scenarios provide tangible reference points for assessing architectural dependencies, integration requirements, and the potential role of AI within a customer’s target landscape.

AI enablement is progressing across the model company portfolio, with capabilities and availability varying by industry and line of business. Their adoption within a customer environment remains subject to scenario availability, release compatibility, licensing and entitlements, technical prerequisites, and applicable AI consumption arrangements.

By combining a clean-core-aligned baseline with activated Joule capabilities and validated AI use cases, model company helps architects bridge the gap between AI strategy and practical enablement.

 

Conclusion: A Better Starting Point for Architectural Decisions

 

Model company changes the starting point, not the architect’s responsibility. Instead of working only from abstract models or a blank configuration, teams can examine a tangible, SAP-delivered baseline and use it to validate assumptions, challenge unnecessary complexity and make more informed Fit-to-Standard decisions.

Whether your role is enterprise architecture or solution architecture, the benefit is a clearer distinction between what the reference already demonstrates, what the customer genuinely needs and what must still be designed and governed.

Start with one critical capability from your target architecture. Explore the model company content available for the relevant industry, test the associated process assumptions and document where the standard fits or where further decisions are needed.

What is the harder challenge in your projects:

  • Validating standard coverage
  • Designing integrations
  • Governing extensions?

Share your experience in the comments.

For availability and request guidance, consult your model company industry/Line of Business dashboard or contact modelcompany@sap.com. For scope selection and applicable terms, refer to SAP Note 3631601 through your normal SAP support channel.

 

Continue the Series

 

If you missed Part 1, read Model company for SAP cloud solutions: Your Fast Track to Fit-to-Standard. Upcoming topics will explore the consultant, partner and content/toolchain perspectives.

 

Further Reading

 

SAP Help Portal: Connecting an SAP Signavio Workspace to SAP Cloud ALM

SAP Help Portal: What is the Extension Architecture Guide?

SAP Help Portal: Side-by-Side Extensibility

About the author: Erik Rahm is Program Manager for model company for SAP cloud solutions at SAP, with more than 30 years of experience in SAP and enterprise transformation.

entry.title: Integrating AI into the Order-to-Cash Process
entry.content:
Innovating Order-to-Cash Teaching with AI

The Order-to-Cash (O2C) process in #SAP S/4HAN represents one of the most important end-to-end business processes in an organization by cutting across multiple business functions—sales, marketing, supply chain, logistics, finance and customer service.. A typical O2C process can be represented as:

Customer Inquiry → Quotation → Sales Order → Availability/ATP → Delivery → Picking & Packing → Goods Issue → Billing → Accounts Receivable → Payment

With O2C process students need to understand why each activity is performed, how information flows across functions, how one decision affects subsequent activities, and how the process ultimately contributes to customer service and business performance.

Students need to understand not only the individual steps but also questions such as:

  • Why is a quotation created before a sales order?
  • Is it necessary to create Inquiry and/or Quotation for creating Sales Order?
  • What information flows from the sales order to delivery?
  • What happens when sufficient inventory is not available?
  • Why does goods issue affect inventory and accounting?
  • How does billing create a financial transaction?
  • What happens to the customer's receivable after billing?
  • What business consequences arise when delivery is delayed?

AI tools like ChatGPT, Claude and Copilot can be integrated at each of these learning points to enhance learning. AI can therefore be positioned as a learning companion around the SAP system, rather than as a replacement for SAP practice. Before entering the system, students can use ChatGPT to explore an Order-to-Cash business scenario, identify relevant process steps and formulate questions that they should investigate in SAP. During the exercise, they can use AI to explore alternative explanations for issues such as incomplete order confirmations, delivery delays, pricing discrepancies or blocked orders. After completing the SAP process, students can use AI to interpret the resulting information, analyse Order-to-Cash data, construct management summaries and reflect on the business implications of their decisions. In this way, AI can help create a continuous learning cycle: understand → investigate → execute → analyse → question → reflect.

The integration of AI also provides an opportunity to make students more actively engaged with SAP by presenting managerial challenges like: A strategic customer requires urgent delivery, but the requested quantity cannot be fully confirmed. What could be causing the problem? What information would you investigate? What alternatives could the company consider? Students can use AI to generate hypotheses, investigate those hypotheses in SAP S/4HANA, use Copilot to analyse relevant data, and then defend their conclusions. The SAP system becomes the evidence base, while AI becomes a tool for exploration and reasoning.

This approach also allows faculty to introduce AI-supported experiential learning into SAP courses. AI tool like ChatGPT can generate different customer and business scenarios, role-play customers or sales managers, create troubleshooting situations and challenge students with follow-up questions. Copilot can support data analysis, visualization and preparation of management-oriented reports using Order-to-Cash data. Students can consequently move from repetitive transaction execution to activities such as diagnosing process problems, comparing alternative decisions, interpreting data and communicating recommendations.

The role of AI, therefore, is not simply to make SAP learning faster or easier. Its greater educational potential lies in shifting the focus from "Can the student execute the transaction correctly?" to broader questions such as "Does the student understand the business process?", "Can the student diagnose what is happening?", "Can the student use data and AI critically?", and "Can the student translate SAP information into a managerial decision?"

Such an approach transforms O2C from a largely transaction-oriented practical exercise into a business simulation and decision-learning experience. Students still develop the essential hands-on SAP skills, but they also develop AI literacy, analytical thinking, problem-solving, business-process understanding and managerial judgment. The objective is not to have AI perform the student's SAP work; rather, it is to use AI to make the student more curious, more analytical and more engaged with the business problem that lies behind the transaction.

 

Some Examples of AI Prompt for O2C Process

  • Act as an SAP business process consultant and ask AI tool to explain the Order-to-Cash process in SAP S/4HANA to an MBA student who understands basic sales and accounting but has never used SAP. Explain the business purpose of each major step and how information flows from one step to another.
  • Asking AI to explain how a sales order, delivery, goods issue, billing document and accounting document are related in an SAP S/4HANA Order-to-Cash process. Give a simple business example
  • Gave students a 3-page customer contract PDF. Ask them to use AI tool to extract SAP SD configuration requirements, create the customer master, and process the order in the live system within defined time frame. Write a summary of learnings.
  • Why can a sales order be created even when the requested quantity is not immediately available?
  • What is the business significance of the delivery block in an O2C process?
  • What could happen to customer satisfaction, inventory and revenue recognition if goods issue is delayed?
  • What happens to the customer's outstanding receivable?
  • A customer order for 500 units has been created, but only 300 units are confirmed for delivery. Identify possible business and SAP-related reasons and explain how a consultant should investigate the issue.
  • Generate five different Order-to-Cash business scenarios for an MBA SAP class. Each scenario should involve a different customer, product, quantity, delivery requirement and business problem. Ensure that the scenarios require students to analyze the implications for sales order, delivery, inventory and billing.
  • A customer has placed an order for 2,000 units. Only 1,200 units are available, the customer has a strict delivery deadline, and the sales manager wants to maximize customer satisfaction without creating excessive inventory pressure. Analyze the situation and recommend how the O2C process should be managed.

 

AI can help in improving Learning Outcomes

  • On-Demand Clarification: Students stuck on why a process steps to be followed in a certain order can ask AI rather than waiting for the next class.
  • Active, Not Passive Learning: Instead of memorizing process sequences, students can use AI to build their own models from SAP export – reinforcing the “Why” behind each transaction.
  • Document-heavy Scenarios Made Traceable: Real Business scenarios involve contracts, RFQs, and invoices. AI allows students practice with realistic, messy documents rather than oversimplified examples.
  • Cross-function thinking: Students can use AI to get clear understanding of cross-functional integrated system process used by O-2-C of SAP.
  • Scenario Variation: Faculty can use AI tool to generate number of different scenarios with varied terms – giving every student a different case and reducing copy-paste submissions.
  • Error-Injection: Faculty can use AI to inject a deliberate errors into a dataset forcing students to identify and correct --- this helps in assessing diagnostic skills.

 

Conclusion

  • The Order-to-Cash process provides an excellent environment for integrating generative AI into SAP education because it combines business processes, transactional data, cross-functional dependencies and managerial decisions.
  • AI tools like ChatGPT can serve as a conceptual tutor, questioning partner, scenario generator and troubleshooting companion, while Microsoft Copilot can add significant value when students work with Excel, PowerPoint, Word and other Microsoft 365-based learning activities and O2C datasets.
  • The ultimate objective, however, should not be to teach students to use AI to complete SAP assignments faster. It should be to teach them to combine AI, SAP and human judgment effectively.

entry.title: V2G integration in IS-U Billing (Part 4): Calculating the availability bonus in Convergent Invoicing
entry.content:
Introduction

In the previous chapters of this series, we explored how a Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) meter-to-cash process can be implemented entirely within SAP IS-U, including the calculation of an availability bonus based on the time a vehicle remains connected to the grid during discharging.

In this final chapter, I would like to explore an alternative approach: leveraging SAP Convergent Invoicing (CI) to calculate the availability bonus while keeping the conventional IS-U metering and billing setup unchanged. Instead of introducing additional configurations in IS-U to register meter-reading results in minutes (MIN), we can use CI to calculate the availability bonus based on the number of hours for which the vehicle was connected to the grid.

Meanwhile, the charging and discharging quantities continue to be registered through a conventional bidirectional meter in kilowatt-hours (kWh).

In other words, our IS-U installation requires only the conventional bidirectional-meter setup for the Meter-to-Cash process.

Bidirectional meter ISU_WALLBOX01 installed in installation 4100000514.

MR-results for charging and discharging registered in kWh.

Billing document 100000005601 – No amount calculated for availability bonus.

The availability bonus will be calculated separately in CI and subsequently integrated into the IS-U invoicing process. But how can we bring these two billing streams together and ensure that the customer receives a single invoice covering both the energy-related charges and the availability bonus?

Let's explore the required configuration and processing steps, from creating and rating consumption items in CI to joint invoicing and the resulting FI-CA postings.

 

1. Consumption Item Class (CIC) and Billable Item Class (BIC) creation

The first step is to configure a new Consumption Item Class (CIC). As a demonstration for this blog, I created a new CIC named “ZV2G”, specifically for the V2G solution.

Customizing path:

Transaction: FICAIMG >> Contract Accounts Receivable and Payable >> Convergent Invoicing >> Basic Functions >> Consumption Items >> Consumption Item classes >> Maintain Consumption Item Classes

Consumption Item class ZV2G

Consumption Item class ZV2G – Interface components.

Once the CIC has been created and its interface generated, the system creates a corresponding database table. In this example, the generated table is /1FC/0ZV2G400.

Consumption Item class ZV2G generated database table - /1FC/0ZV2G400.

This table stores the consumption items belonging to the class, including items created for testing and simulation. After rating, the corresponding rating results can be examined in the relevant records.

Examples of entries created after simulation runs.

Once the consumption items (CIT) have been rated, the system generates the resulting billable items, which can be processed further in Convergent Invoicing through billing execution. For this scenario, however, I also configured integrated billing, which allows the billing document to be created as part of the rating process in my setup.

To support the V2G integration, I created a corresponding Billable Item Class (BIC), also named ZV2G.

Customizing path:

Transaction: FICAIMG >> Contract Accounts Receivable and Payable >> Convergent Invoicing >> Basic Functions >> Billable Items >> Billable Item classes >> Maintain Billable Item Classes

Billable Item class ZV2G.

Billable Item class ZV2G – Database table /1FE/0ZV2G4IT00.

Billable Item class ZV2G – interface components.

It is important to note that this V2G blog post does not aim to explain every aspect of CIC and BIC configuration. The exact configuration depends on the intended integration scenario, the selected interface components, and the requirements of the implementation.

However, for a more detailed introduction to Convergent Invoicing and its integration with Utilities, I highly recommend the blog series by Oleh Korolyk, beginning with his article:

SAP Billing and Revenue Innovation Management: commodity and non-commodity services on one (or separate) invoice is no longer a dream

The article provides an excellent starting point and contains all the links to all other posts in his series.

I highly recommend reading this blog series as well!

2. Pricing and Rating Configurations

As discussed in the previous chapter, the availability bonus in our example is calculated using a price of −0.24 per hour (HR).

To implement this calculation in Convergent invoicing, I configured a pricing procedure for the relevant posting area 8200. This can be done by following the customizing path below:

Transaction: FICAIMG >> Contract Accounts Receivable and Payable >> Convergent Invoicing >> Basic Functions >> Pricing >> Assigning Pricing schemas

For this example, I used pricing procedure CI1001, which is an SD pricing procedure that can be maintained using transaction V/08. A pricing procedure defines the sequence of condition types and calculation steps used to determine the applicable price.

Pricing procedures CI1001 with the condition types configured in its steps.

For this example, I used condition type PST0 to maintain the price applied when rating the consumption items. The condition record can be maintained using transaction VK11, with the relevant combination of sales organization, distribution channel, customer, material, and price unit, according to the condition type configuration.

Price condition within condition type PST0.

Configurations of material EXTM – Transaction MM03.

Once the SD pricing configuration is complete, we must ensure that the relevant pricing logic is executed when the consumption items are rated.

 For this purpose, I assigned the function module ‘FKK_BIX_RATING_EVENT_30_SD’ in the program extensions of the newly created rating group RV2G.

Customizing path:

Transaction: FICAIMG >> Contract Accounts Receivable and Payable >> Convergent Invoicing >> Rating >> Define Rating Groups

I then assigned our newly created Consumption Item Class ZV2G to the rating group RV2G:

Customizing path:

Transaction: FICAIMG >> Contract Accounts Receivable and Payable >> Convergent Invoicing >> Rating >> Assign Consumption Item Classes to Rating Groups

With these settings in place, the consumption items can be rated using the configured pricing logic.

The negative price represents the customer credit in this example. The resulting amount must be verified against the actual pricing and posting configuration to ensure that the availability bonus is represented correctly in the subsequent billing and FI-CA documents.

3. Provider contract for the availability bonus

After completing the required CI configuration, we can create the provider contract for the relevant business partner. For this purpose, I used transaction FP_VT1.

The provider contract must contain the relevant account and commercial assignments required by the pricing and rating configuration. In this example, these include the business partner, contract account, company code, sales organization, distribution channel, and material.

Provider contract V2G_AVLB – General Data.

The provider contract V2G_AVLB is linked to contract account 200000003200.

Provider contract V2G_AVLB – General Data: Linked to contract account 200000003200.

In the account assignment data, the provider contract is linked to sales organization 2510, company code BCMP, and product EXTM.

Provider contract V2G_AVLB – Account Assignment: Linked to Sales org. 2510; Company code BCMP and Product EXTM (MM).

These assignments allow the consumption items to be associated with the relevant customer account and commercial data used for pricing.

4. Creation and Rating of Consumption Items

Once the provider contract has been created, we can create a consumption item using transaction FKKBIXCIT_CWB.

 For this demonstration, I created the consumption item manually and linked it to the provider contract. The following information can then be specified:

  • Consumption date
  • Unit of measurement (UoM)
  • Quantity consumed
  • Consumption item type

The unit of measurement (UoM) specified in the consumption item must be compatible with the pricing configuration. Since our availability bonus is calculated per hour, I used HR as the unit of measurement.

Consumption Item 2608230005000000600001

In this example, we create the consumption items manually. In a production environment, however, consumption items would typically be created automatically from data received from an external application. For example, a charging station provider could supply the connection duration of a vehicle through an integration interface.

The interface would need to transform and validate the incoming data before creating the corresponding consumption items in your SAP S/4HANA system.

SAP provides APIs for creating consumption items. The exact API to use depends on the interface generated for the consumption item class and the SAP release. For the ZV2G class, the generated interface and its supported usage should be verified before implementation.

One option would be the general API ‘FKK_BIX_CIT_CREATE_API ‘:

Function Module FKK_BIX_CIT_CREATE_API in which function ‘FKK_BIX_CIT_CREATE’ is called.

Alternatively, SAP can generate a class-specific RFC function module for each Consumption Item Class, following the naming convention /1FC/XXX_CIT_CREATE_API. These generated interfaces are adapted to the structure of the corresponding class.

For our example, after generating the interfaces for CIC ZV2G, the system created the Function Module ‘/1FC/ZV2G_CIT_CREATE_API’, which is tailored to the structure of CIC ZV2G.

Function Module /1FC/ZV2G_CIT_CREATE_API adapted to the structure of CIC ZV2G.

Once the Consumption Item has been created, we can execute rating.

After successful rating, the consumption item receives the corresponding rated status:

Consumption item 2608230005000000600001 with status “Rated”.

In a conventional CI process, rating produces billable items that are subsequently processed during billing. As mentioned before, in my example, the rating group is configured for integrated billing, so the billing document is created as part of the configured rating process.

Consequently, there is no need to execute a separate billable-item billing run using transaction FKKBIXBIT_MON for this particular scenario.

This behavior depends on the integrated-billing configuration and should not be assumed for every CI implementation:

Transaction: FICAIMG >> Contract Accounts Receivable and Payable >> Convergent Invoicing >> Rating >> Define Rating Groups

The resulting billing document contains the calculated availability bonus. It also carries the quantity and unit of measurement entered in the consumption item, provided the relevant billing-quantity interface component is selected in the billable item class.

Billing document 347 including amount, quantity, and unit of measurement.

Billable Item Class ZV2G with interface component “Billing quantity”.

This completes the CI calculation of the availability bonus. The next step is to integrate the resulting billing document into the IS-U invoicing process.

5. Executing the invoicing run in IS-U

We now have two billing documents:

  • An IS-U billing document containing the charging and discharging quantities measured in kWh.
  • A CI billing document containing the availability bonus calculated from the connection duration.

The objective is to process both documents through IS-U invoicing so that the resulting customer invoice includes both components.

To ensure that both billing documents can be invoiced together, you need to customize the invoicing process in which you can specify the source document categories in the selection control.

Once your invoicing process is defined in the customizing, you also need to specify to which creation reason in IS-U it applies. For our scenario, we want our CI billing document to be invoiced on the same print document together with an IS-U billing document with source document type “01”:

EAINV_MON – Source document type.

When you invoice the contract account via transaction EAINV_MON, you will be asked to specify the invoicing process along with its compatible creation reason. After executing, the system will at one point call function ISU_INV_SELECT_DOCUMENTS which verifies whether the selected invoicing process is compatible with the creation reason of the IS-U billing document:

Function Module ISU_INV_SELECT_DOCUMENTS with CALL FUNCTION ‘ISU_DB_TE2602_SELECT’ on line 82.

As illustrated by the image above, the assignment between the creation reason and the invoicing process is stored in table TE2602:

Table TE2602: Assignment of invoicing procedure to creation reason.

If the required assignment is missing, the CI billing document may not be selected for joint invoicing through the intended IS-U invoicing process.

The relevant customizing activity is:

SAP Customizing Implementation Guide >> SAP Utilities >> Invoicing >> Integration with Convergent Invoicing >> Invoicing of Source Documents from Convergent Invoicing >> Assign Invoicing Process to Reasons for Creation

Once the required configuration is in place, the joint invoicing run can be executed. In my example, both transactions EAINV_MON and EA19 can be used to produce the joint invoicing result:

Joint invoicing of billing documents 347 (CI) and 100000005601 (IS-U) through EAINV_MON.

Joint invoicing of both billing documents 347 (CI) and 100000005601 (IS-U) through EA19.

Although both transactions produce the same result, I prefer EAINV_MON because it displays additional information such as target process. 

After executing the invoicing run and selecting the relevant source documents, the system successfully creates IS-U print document 2000000229:

Application log – print document 2000000229 successfully created.

By navigating to the Source Documents tab of the print document, we can identify the billing documents included in the invoicing process. In this example, the print document references the IS-U billing document 100000005601 (ERCH) and the CI billing document 347 (INVBI):

IS-U Print Document 2000000229 with source documents 100000005601 (ERCH) and 347 (INVBI).

This confirms that the two billing results have been brought together in a common IS-U invoicing process.

6. Final results: IS-U print document, Invoicing document and FI-CA posting documents

After successful joint invoicing, we can examine the resulting documents to understand how the IS-U and CI components are represented in the system.

6.1 IS-U Print Document

The resulting IS-U print document is 2000000229.

Its document overview shows the posting-relevant items originating from the IS-U billing process and the availability bonus calculated through CI.

IS-U Print document 2000000229 - Document Overview.

As shown in the image above, I did not apply any tax amounts for the availability bonus just as I did in the previous part of this series (V2G integration in IS-U Billing (Part 3) : From Measured Quantities to Billing and Invoicing). For the invoicing document that will be created through CI, you can configure this in posting area 2610 by linking the required tax determination to your company code, main and sub-transactions and the targeted G/L account for postings to be made.

Account assignments on chart of accounts 2500 in posting area 2610.

6.2. CI Invoicing Document

The IS-U print document also provides a link to the associated CI invoicing document.

In this example, the CI invoicing document number is 7000000116. It can be identified through the relevant reference field in table ERDK in the demonstrated system.

Invoicing document 7000000116 in table field ERDK- INVDOCNO.

To examine the document in more detail, we can use transaction FKKINVDOC_DISP.

The CI invoicing document contains the relevant invoicing information for the availability bonus, including the items processed through CI and the applicable integration information.

Invoicing document 7000000116 in FKKINVDOC_DISP.

This provides a useful way to trace the availability bonus from its original consumption item through rating and billing to the final invoicing result.

6.3. FI-CA Posting Documents

Finally, we can examine the FI-CA postings created as part of the invoicing process.

In this example, the system creates two FI-CA posting documents: one for the items originating from IS-U and another for the availability bonus originating from CI.

The documents are 5000000702 and 5000000703, and both refer to the common IS-U print document 2000000229:

Two documents posted in FI-CA:  5000000702 and 5000000703.

Table DFKKOP: posting documents 5000000702 and 5000000703 representing the total amount of IS-U print document 2000000229.

This distinction is important. Although the customer-facing result is a common IS-U print document, the underlying financial processing can retain separate FI-CA documents for the IS-U and CI components.

The example therefore illustrates how the availability bonus can be calculated independently in CI and integrated into the IS-U invoicing process without requiring both components to originate from the same billing engine.

 

Conclusion

With this final chapter, we have explored an alternative approach to integrating a V2G availability bonus into the SAP IS-U Meter-to-Cash process by leveraging Convergent Invoicing.

By retaining the conventional IS-U metering and billing setup for charging and discharging quantities in kWh, we can calculate the availability bonus separately in CI based on the vehicle's connection time. The resulting CI billing document can then be integrated into the IS-U invoicing process, allowing both billing results to be included in a common IS-U print document.

We have also followed the process beyond billing and invoicing, examining the resulting CI invoicing document and the separate FI-CA postings generated for the IS-U and CI components.

This approach demonstrates one possible way to combine the capabilities of SAP IS-U and Convergent Invoicing while avoiding additional IS-U configuration to register the availability duration in minutes.

I hope this four-part V2G series has provided useful insights into the different possibilities for implementing Vehicle-to-Grid scenarios in SAP Utilities.

Thank you for following the series! I would be very interested to hear your thoughts:

Would you implement the availability bonus directly in IS-U, or would you consider Convergent Invoicing for this purpose?

Feel free to share your experiences and alternative approaches in the comments.

entry.title: Stop Building SAP Apps: Business AI Applications On Demand with an Ontology-Based MCP Server
entry.content:
Apps on demand instead of app projects

A sales rep desk for delivery-blocked orders on SAP ECC took us a few hours to build, not a project. It runs on live SAP data, follows the team's process step by step and writes back to SAP only after the rep confirms.

The usual route looks different. A new cockpit for one team starts a cycle of requirements, functional and technical specifications, OData services, a Fiori or UI5 front end, testing and transports. Weeks pass, and the team keeps working in reports, spreadsheets and email.

We took a typical wholesale scenario, connected Claude Desktop to the Skybuffer AI MCP server, our ABAP add-on, and asked for the application with nothing but the process description. This post shows what came out, the two architectures it runs on, and why the MCP server, more than the AI model, decides whether this works.

The example: a release desk for delivery block 17

The desk works the orders that SAP holds on delivery block 17 ("CSR action: deadline") because their cancel date is close. Each one needs a decision before that date, and the desk takes the customer service rep through all eight steps of the process on one screen, with live SAP data at every step.

The worklist: twelve orders on block 17, sorted by days to the cancel date, with stock coverage per order and a count of orders at each step.

StepWhat the rep sees and doesSkybuffer AI MCP tool
1. IdentifyEvery open order on the block, sorted by days left to the cancel date, with filters for overdue, due within two days and ready to releaseget_blocked_sales_orders
2. Check stockPer line: ordered quantity, available to promise, shortfall and the next incoming receipt; stock on hand per plantget_blocked_sales_orders, get_material_stock
3. DecideSAP's recommendation (release, extend, partial ship or cancel) with a plain-language reason; the rep makes the callget_blocked_sales_orders
4. Contact the customerOne email draft per customer, addressed to the buyer from SAP, covering all of their orders on hold with PO numbers, account executive in copyget_customers_contact_details
5. Customer replyThe answer is logged with a note, and a reply-by date drives a follow-up list(kept by the app)
6. Update SAPNew requested date, rejected lines with a reason, block kept or removed; every change shown in a confirmation dialog first, then read back from SAPchange_sales_order, get_sales_order_status
7. ReleaseBlock 17 removed, the order goes to the warehousechange_sales_order
8. Follow upOrders without an answer by the reply date come back as a chase list(kept by the app)

Steps 2 and 3: availability per line, stock on hand and SAP's recommendation with its reason. Here SAP suggests a partial shipment, and the rep picks the line to cancel.

When stock covers every line before the cancel date, SAP recommends a release instead. The customer doesn't need to hear from us, so the desk skips the email and lets the rep remove the block straight away.

Every line is available before the cancel date, so SAP suggests a release and no customer contact is needed.

Nobody wrote UI code by hand. Claude Desktop generated the application from the eight-step process description and the tool descriptions the MCP server publishes. The first version ran within a few hours of the first prompt, and we refined it over the same day.

Two rules held throughout. Nothing changes in SAP without the rep's confirmation, and customer emails are only drafted, never sent by the app.

Step 4: one draft per customer for all of their orders on hold, with the buyer's address from SAP and the account executive in copy. Nothing is sent from the page.

Step 6: before posting, the rep sees each change in plain words and the exact MCP call behind it.

Why the MCP server needs a business ontology, not an OData wrapper

The model can only build an app as good as the tools it is given. An MCP server that wraps OData services hands the model database entities; an MCP server built on a business ontology hands it the process itself.

By ontology we mean the shared vocabulary of the business: the objects (customer, sales order, line, delivery block, cancel date, availability, inbound receipt), how they relate, the actions allowed on them and the rules behind those actions. When the tools speak that vocabulary, the steps of the app can match the steps of the process one to one.

 OData wrapperBusiness ontology MCP server
A tool representsAn entity set: order headers, items, schedule linesA business capability: find blocked orders and assess them against their cancel date
Who joins the dataThe model, call by call: header, items, schedule lines, availability, stock listThe server, inside SAP, in one call
Business rulesRebuilt by the model each time: confirmations, rejected lines, units of measureImplemented once in ABAP with standard BAPIs
What comes backRaw fields such as VDATU, LIFSK, KWMENGAnswer-ready fields: days to cancel, coverage, next inbound date, recommended action and its reason
WritesA generic update on an entity; the model must know update flags and schedule linesBusiness actions: move the requested date and keep the block, reject lines with a reason, remove the block
AuthorizationsPer servicePer action and per order, checked against the user's SAP roles on every call

The difference shows in the numbers. The desk's worklist of twelve orders, with availability per line and a recommendation per order, comes from a single call. Built on entity reads, the same screen needs several reads per order plus an availability check per line, and every join is a chance for the model to get it wrong.

Every call goes to the live system, so the app works in real time. Nothing is replicated into a data lake or a side database, and SAP stays the system of record.

Architecture 1: the ABAP add-on and Claude Desktop

The simplest setup has two parts: Claude Desktop on the user's machine and the Skybuffer AI MCP server, installed as an ABAP add-on in the SAP system itself.

Architecture 1: Claude Desktop and the ABAP MCP add-on

The rep works in Claude Desktop and signs in to SAP through SSO with their own SAP user, so there is no shared technical user. Every tool call goes over HTTPS to the add-on, which runs the business logic inside SAP with standard BAPIs and checks that user's SAP authorizations before it returns or changes anything.

The add-on's MCP endpoint is an ICF node in the SAP system. Claude reaches it as a remote MCP connector, and connector calls come from Claude's cloud, so the ICF node is published through your reverse proxy or a secure tunnel; in Architecture 2, the gateway takes that role.

There is no middleware to install, no data replication and no separate app server. The add-on runs on SAP ECC and on SAP S/4HANA, with S/4HANA variants where the data model differs, so the app moves with the system through a migration.

This setup suits pilots, departmental apps and any team that wants the shortest path from an idea to a working app.

Architecture 2: SAP BTP with the MCP Gateway in the middle

Companies that standardize on SAP BTP can put the MCP Gateway in SAP Integration Suite, announced at SAP TechEd 2025, between Claude and the add-on. The app and the tools stay exactly the same; the gateway adds central governance.

Architecture 2: SAP BTP with the MCP Gateway in the middle

Claude calls the gateway with the user's identity. The gateway applies its policies and forwards the call through SAP Cloud Connector, and the add-on runs the same tools as in Architecture 1.

What the SAP-endorsed path adds, as SAP's reference architecture describes it:

  • One governed entry point for MCP tools, including external MCP servers such as the Skybuffer AI add-on
  • OAuth 2.0 and OIDC enforcement, rate limiting, payload protection and traffic management
  • Monitoring, distributed tracing and analytics in one place
  • Tool lifecycle from creation to versioning and deprecation, with MCP specification upgrades handled by SAP

The SAP system itself stays behind the firewall: SAP Cloud Connector opens an outbound tunnel to BTP, so no inbound port is needed.

The gateway can also turn existing APIs and integration flows into MCP tools. That is handy for simple reads, but for a process like this one it brings back the OData-wrapper problem. The split that works: the gateway governs the call, and the business ontology lives in the MCP server behind it.

The Skybuffer AI MCP server and its predefined tools

Both architectures run on the same MCP server: the Skybuffer AI MCP server, an ABAP add-on from Skybuffer that implements MCP inside SAP ECC and SAP S/4HANA. It is built on SAP technology only, so any SAP team or partner can support it.

Out of the box, the server comes with predefined business tools. Each one is a business capability, such as reading a customer's contacts, checking stock or creating a purchase requisition, written in ABAP on a common framework and published with a description that tells the model when and how to use it.

Predefined tools are why an app takes hours instead of weeks:

  • Most of the app already exists. The desk reuses predefined tools for customer contacts, stock, order status and governed data access. Only two tools were new for this scenario, get_blocked_sales_orders and change_sales_order, and both are now part of the standard content.
  • Business logic is built once, tested and shared. Availability, confirmations, rejection reasons and units of measure are handled in ABAP with standard BAPIs instead of being reinvented by the model in every app. Two apps never disagree about the same order, and an improvement to a tool reaches every app that uses it.
  • Security comes with every call. Each tool checks the user's SAP authorizations before it reads or changes anything, and changes are recorded in the SAP application log. A new app inherits these controls instead of rebuilding them.
  • IT stays in control. Customizing decides which tools are active and which tables and views the data access tool may read, each with its own field list and record limit.

When a process needs something new, the new tool is one more ABAP class on the same framework, registered in customizing and transported like any other ABAP change. The server publishes it to every MCP client automatically, so the next app can use it the same day.

Distributing the app across the company

The desk is a published page on claude.ai, so rolling it out means sharing a link, not deploying an application. Claude artifacts on Team and Enterprise plans provide everything the rollout needs.

  1. Each user connects the Skybuffer AI connector once in Claude, under Settings > Connectors, and signs in through SSO with their own SAP user.
  2. The author shares the page with named colleagues or with the whole organization. Viewers sign in to Claude, on the desktop app or the web.
  3. An Owner keeps control in the admin settings: artifacts on or off, connector calls from artifacts on or off, and public sharing, which is off by default.

Once shared, these rules hold:

  • Every viewer sees their own SAP. Each connector call runs through the viewer's own connection, so two reps with different SAP roles see different orders. The page never sees credentials, and each viewer approves access before the first call.
  • Actions run as the person who clicks. A release, a new date or a rejected line is posted under that user's SAP account and authorizations.
  • The team shares one picture. Decisions, customer replies, notes and the activity feed are kept with the app, while SAP data is read live for each viewer.
  • Updates reach everyone. Each republish becomes a new version on the same link, and the owner chooses which version viewers see.
  • Governance is built in. Artifacts are visible only to signed-in members of the organization and the people they are shared with, and they fall under retention policies, the audit log and the Compliance API.

Conclusion: fast, cheap and built to SAP standards

With a proper MCP server and Claude Desktop, a business AI app stops being a project. A team describes its process in the morning and works in the app in the afternoon, on live SAP data.

 Classic app projectBusiness AI app on demand
First versionWeeks of specification, development and testingA few hours
Built byA development teamA consultant or power user with Claude Desktop
New to deployOData services, a Fiori or UI5 app, transportsNothing, once the add-on is in place: the app is a shared link
Fit to the processAs specified at the startBuilt from the process description, refined the same day
DataOften copied for reportingLive from SAP ECC or S/4HANA
A changeA change requestA prompt, republished to the same link

Fast. Apps arrive in hours, and changes the same day.

Cheap. Architecture 1 needs no middleware and no extra runtime, only the ABAP add-on in the existing system and Claude for the users. There is no UI code or OData layer to maintain, most tools come predefined with the server, and each new one is reused by the next app.

Very good quality. The logic runs in SAP through standard BAPIs and SAP authorization checks. Every change is confirmed by a person and read back, and the app follows the process because it was built from it.

The same approach works on SAP ECC today and on SAP S/4HANA after the migration. The Skybuffer AI MCP server is not tied to one client either: Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini and VS Code can all use the same tools. Start with Architecture 1 for speed, and move to Architecture 2 when the rollout needs SAP BTP governance.

  • Skybuffer: MCP server for SAP ECC and S/4HANA
