entry.title: Building an AI-Powered SAP BASIS Operations Assistant with MCP, Python and PyRFC
entry.content:
1. Introduction

What if SAP BASIS administrators/consultants could ask an AI assistant “Are there any ST22 dumps today?”, “Which background jobs failed?”, or “Show me the busiest users in ST03N”, and receive live data from an SAP system rather than generic troubleshooting advice?

This article documents a working proof of concept that connects ChatGPT to an on-premise SAP S/4HANA 2023 system through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), Python, PyRFC and SAP NetWeaver RFC SDK. The integration currently exposes six read-oriented operational tools. It does not require SAP BTP, SAP Cloud Connector or OData for its RFC-based architecture.

The focus is reproducible architecture, actual implementation details, lessons learned and the security boundaries needed before considering production deployment.

2. Architecture

The MCP listener is bound to loopback, not the VM LAN interface. This reduces direct network exposure, but does not itself authenticate remote users. The tested plugin was configured without authentication; that setting is appropriate only for a tightly controlled PoC, not a shared or production service.

3. Tested environment

The following components were used in the working proof of concept:

SAP System: SAP S/4HANA 2023, SID S4D, ABAP 7.58, SAP HANA, client 100.

SAP Application Instance: Instance number 01, private lab network.

MCP Server: Rocky Linux 9.8 running on Microsoft Hyper-V.

Python Runtime: Python 3.11 virtual environment.

PyRFC: Version 3.4.

SAP NetWeaver RFC SDK: Version 7.50, PL20.

MCP Python SDK: Version 2.3.0.

MCP Transport: Streamable HTTP, listening on 127.0.0.1:8000/mcp.

SAP RFC User: Dedicated technical user (MCP_RFC).

Linux Service Accounts: sapmcp for the HTTP service and mcpadmin for the tunnel service.

This configuration was validated in a dedicated lab environment and should be treated as a proof of concept rather than a production-ready deployment.

4. Preparing the Linux environment

The installation uses /opt/sap-mcp. The commands below are safe verification commands for the actual environment, not a reconstructed history of every dnf or pip operation.

Project structure, omitting backup files, logs, credentials and the virtual environment:

/opt/sap-mcp/
  app/
    server.py
    server_http.py
    test_mcp.py
    test_mcp_http.py
  config/
    sap.env              # private; never publish contents
  packages/
    pyrfc-3.4-cp311-cp311-linux_x86_64.whl
  venv/
  tests/
    test_rfc.py

For a new installation, install the SAP NetWeaver RFC SDK using SAP-authorized distribution and its supported platform instructions. Install a Python version compatible with the chosen PyRFC wheel, and ensure the RFC SDK shared libraries are discoverable by the service process. The original package installation transcript and runtime library-path settings were not preserved in the reviewed documentation; therefore this article does not invent exact commands for those steps.

5. SAP RFC connection and credential handling

A dedicated technical SAP user in client 100 is used for RFC calls. Credentials are loaded from a private environment file outside the source code. Example variable names (values intentionally omitted):

SAP_ASHOST=<sap-application-host>
SAP_SYSNR=01
SAP_CLIENT=100
SAP_USER=<dedicated-rfc-user>
SAP_PASSWORD=<secret>
SAP_LANG=EN

sudo stat -c "%U %G %a %n" /opt/sap-mcp/config/sap.env

The working deployment uses restrictive permissions (mode 600). Never paste the actual environment file into a blog, issue tracker, AI prompt or screenshot. Grant only required RFC and application authorizations; RFC-enabled does not automatically mean read-only, released or safe for external use.

6. MCP server design

The application registers Python functions with an MCP server named SAP-S4D-Operations using @McP.tool(). A typical tool validates input, opens a PyRFC connection, calls an SAP function module, converts the result to JSON-compatible data and closes the connection.

In the real application, connection parameters are constructed by a load_config() helper and tools are registered using the MCP decorator. Inspect SAP function signatures in SE37 and, where useful, through PyRFC function metadata. Test function behavior in SAP before exposing it as a tool.

7. HTTP entry point — verified source

This code was copied from the running /opt/sap-mcp/app/server_http.py:

import asyncio
from server import mcp
if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(
        mcp.run_streamable_http_async(
            host="127.0.0.1",
            port=8000,
            streamable_http_path="/mcp",
        )
    )

The MCP endpoint is http://127.0.0.1:8000/mcp on the Linux VM. An outbound tunnel connects this local service to the remote client integration. The public endpoint and tunnel credentials are intentionally excluded.

8. systemd services — verified configuration

Two services were confirmed active with systemctl is-active: sap-mcp-http.service and sap-mcp-tunnel.service.

8.1 HTTP service

[Unit]
Description=SAP S4D MCP HTTP Server
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target
[Service]
Type=simple
User=sapmcp
Group=sapmcp
WorkingDirectory=/opt/sap-mcp/app
ExecStart=/opt/sap-mcp/venv/bin/python /opt/sap-mcp/app/server_http.py
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5
UMask=0077
NoNewPrivileges=true
[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

8.2 Tunnel service

The following represents the verified service with the local tunnel profile name generalized for publication. A tunnel client must be installed and provisioned separately; its configuration is provider-specific.

[Unit]
Description=Tunnel Client for SAP S4D MCP
Wants=network-online.target
After=network-online.target sap-mcp-http.service
Requires=sap-mcp-http.service
[Service]
Type=simple
User=mcpadmin
Group=mcpadmin
WorkingDirectory=/home/mcpadmin
Environment=HOME=/home/mcpadmin
EnvironmentFile=/etc/tunnel-client/runtime.env
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/tunnel-client run --profile <profile-name>
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=10
UMask=0077
NoNewPrivileges=true

The path to runtime.env is shown only as a configuration location. Do not publish its contents. The service naming and tunnel executable are specific to this PoC; adapt them to the tunnel provider used in your environment.

sudo systemctl is-active sap-mcp-http.service sap-mcp-tunnel.service
sudo systemctl status sap-mcp-http.service --no-pager
sudo systemctl status sap-mcp-tunnel.service --no-pager
sudo ss -lntp | grep :8000
sudo journalctl -u sap-mcp-http.service -n 80 --no-pager

9. The six implemented SAP operations tools

MCP toolSAP capability / implementation
sap_system_infoRFC_SYSTEM_INFO: system metadata
sap_background_jobsBAPI_XMI_LOGON + BAPI_XBP_JOB_SELECT: background jobs
sap_st22_dumpsZ_MCP_ST22_READ: ST22 dumps via internal SAP FM
sap_logged_on_usersActive SAP user sessions; exact SAP FM omitted pending source verification
sap_work_processesTH_WPINFO: work process overview (SM50)
sap_workload_statisticsSWNC_COLLECTOR_GET_AGGREGATES: ST03N daily workload

All six tools have been exercised in the PoC. This table describes operational monitoring, not a generic authorization to execute arbitrary commands or modify SAP data.

10. ST22: a custom RFC-enabled ABAP wrapper

The standard RS_ST22_GET_DUMPS function was not callable directly over RFC in this environment. A custom Remote-Enabled Function Module Z_MCP_ST22_READ was therefore created in function group ZMCP_MONITOR. The PoC used local package $TMP, which is not transportable.

The confirmed ABAP implementation is reproduced below; the FM interface includes IV_DATE, EV_COUNT and ET_DUMPS with types defined in the SAP system:

FUNCTION Z_MCP_ST22_READ.
  DATA: lv_date TYPE sy-datum,
        lt_dumps TYPE rsdumptab.
  CLEAR ev_count.
  REFRESH et_dumps.
  lv_date = iv_date.
  IF lv_date IS INITIAL.
    lv_date = sy-datum.
  ENDIF.
  CALL FUNCTION 'RS_ST22_GET_DUMPS'
    EXPORTING p_day = lv_date
    IMPORTING p_infotab = lt_dumps
    EXCEPTIONS no_authority = 1 OTHERS = 2.
  IF sy-subrc <> 0.
    RETURN.
  ENDIF.
  LOOP AT lt_dumps INTO DATA(ls_dump).
    APPEND ls_dump TO et_dumps.
  ENDLOOP.
  ev_count = lines( et_dumps ).
ENDFUNCTION.

Important limitation: this PoC code returns zero results for both an empty dump list and some failures, including authorization errors. A production wrapper must explicitly propagate errors, validate input, apply authorization checks and avoid returning sensitive dump content unnecessarily.

11. ST03N workload statistics: implementation and validation

The newest tool, sap_workload_statistics(date, top_n=10), reads daily workload aggregates through SWNC_COLLECTOR_GET_AGGREGATES. The tested parameters were COMPONENT=TOTAL, ASSIGNDSYS=S4D, PERIODTYPE=D, PERIODSTRT=<YYYYMMDD>, SUMMARY_ONLY blank, STORAGE_TYPE=A and FACTOR=1000.

The USERTCODE aggregate (DDIC structure SWNCAGGUSERTCODE) is grouped by ACCOUNT. The Python tool sums COUNT, RESPTI, CPUTI, PROCTI and QUEUETI, and converts duration units for the returned report. It validates date format and limits top_n to 1–50.

Validation: 12 October 2026Observed result
Test accountDDIC
Dialog steps8,877
Total response time2,710.256 seconds
Average response time305.31 ms
Total CPU time743.270 seconds
SAP FM records read142

The figures were cross-checked against the SAP GUI ST03N display for the same date and account. Subsequent live MCP tests returned 46,189 total steps for 12 October and 46,429 for 13 October. These are daily totals; the current tool does not establish the busiest hour.

12. Testing end to end

Validate Python syntax, restart the HTTP service after code changes, and run the MCP HTTP test script:

sudo -u sapmcp -H /opt/sap-mcp/venv/bin/python -m py_compile /opt/sap-mcp/app/server.py
sudo systemctl restart sap-mcp-http.service
sudo systemctl status sap-mcp-http.service --no-pager
sudo -u sapmcp -H /opt/sap-mcp/venv/bin/python /opt/sap-mcp/app/test_mcp_http.py

A previously confirmed HTTP test returned the MCP tool list and RFC system information (S4D, ABAP 758, HDB, client 100). After registering new tools, refresh the tool list in the ChatGPT MCP plugin configuration; otherwise the client may continue showing a cached list.

Suggested test prompts: “Show ST22 dumps for 2026-10-13”; “List background jobs for today”; “Show current work processes”; “Summarize ST03N workload for 2026-10-12, top 5 users.” Results depend on RFC authorizations and available SAP data.

13. Troubleshooting lessons

Non-RFC-enabled SAP functions: a direct remote call may produce CALL_FUNCTION_NOT_REMOTE. Verify the FM attributes in SE37; where justified, create a narrow, audited RFC wrapper rather than assuming an internal FM is remotely callable.

Tool visibility: a successful server restart does not necessarily update the ChatGPT plugin tool catalog. Refresh tools and rerun the listing test.

Python decorator behavior: in this implementation, a registered tool function can be called directly for a local test; do not assume it has an .fn property.

ST03N aggregation: match the aggregation period, component and SAP GUI filters before comparing results. A daily aggregate cannot answer a peak-hour question.

14. Security and production readiness

This is a functional PoC, not a production-certified integration. Before deployment to clients, implement authenticated access to the MCP endpoint (for example OAuth/OIDC where supported), per-user and per-system authorization, least-privilege SAP technical users, controlled tool allowlists, auditing, rate limits, secret rotation, network segmentation and response redaction.

For potentially destructive operations such as restart, backup, user administration or job cancellation, introduce explicit approval gates, scoped permissions, precondition checks and change logs. Never expose arbitrary RFC or operating-system command execution merely because an AI client can call tools.

Review SAP support and release status for each function module. Internal SAP FMs may change across releases and are not equivalent to stable public APIs.

15. Next steps

Planned extensions include RFC metadata discovery, SM12 locks, SM21 system logs, ST02/ST06 performance monitoring, hourly ST03N time profiles, and a multi-system gateway with strict system-level isolation. A separate SAP BTP/OData-based MCP integration is also being considered; it has not been implemented as part of this RFC PoC.

16. Conclusion

MCP provides a practical interface between conversational AI and SAP BASIS operations. In this PoC, Python and PyRFC translate six well-defined monitoring tasks into SAP RFC calls, while Streamable HTTP and an outbound tunnel connect the Linux gateway to ChatGPT. The key engineering lesson is to validate SAP APIs, restrict privileges and verify results against SAP GUI before trusting AI-generated operational summaries.

entry.title: Comprehensive guide for configuring and testing 2-step Intercompany STO process with Dlv Ty NCC3
entry.content:
This blog is intended to enable FICO/MM consultants to successfully configure intercompany STO process with delivery type NCC3(stock transfer from the valuated stock in transit of the issuing plant via the valuated stock in transit of the receiving plant to the unrestricted-use stock of the receiving plant) and run an end to end test based on the setup.

Content:

Part A. Configuration Overview:

Part B. Configuration Detail:

Part C. Data Preparation:

Part D. Defects and Solutions

We developed the configurations, master data, and transactional documents in this guide within an SAP S/4HANA 2020 On-Premise (FPS0) environment.

 

Part A. Configuration Overview:

  1. Define (Purchasing) Document Types(ZNB2)
  2. Define Shipping Data for Plants(Receiving Plant 1310 -> Customer No. IC1310, Supplying Plant 1710 -> Sales Organization 1710 + Distribution Channel 10 + Division 00)
  3. Assign Document Type, One-Step Procedure, Underdelivery Tolerance (Supplying Plant 1710 +Receiving Plant 1310 -> STO Document Type ZNB2)
  4. Configure Delivery Type & Availability Check Procedure by Plant(Purchasing Document Type ZNB2 + Supplying Plant 1710 -> Delivery Type NCC3 + Checking Rule B)
  5. Define Item Category Determination in Deliveries( Delivery Type NCC3 + Item Category Group NORM from Material Master Data + Usage V is constant for STO -> Item Category NCC3)
  6. Define Schedule Line Categories( Schedule Line Category N3 -> Movement type 681 & 685)
  7. Assign Schedule Line Categories( Item Category NCC3 + MRP Type Blank -> Schedule Line Category N3 )
  8. Maintain Copying Control for Billing Documents （Tgt IV <- Source NCC3 ）
  9. Define MM Condition Type(PI01) and SD Condition Type (PI01, Refer to MM Condition Type PI01)
  10. Partner Determination Procedure(For Customer/Delivery/Billing)
  11. Define and Assign (SD) Pricing Procedure(To Billing Type IV) （Sales Organization 1310 +Distribution Channel 10+Division 00+ Doc.Pricing Proc. 01+ Cust.Pricing Proc. 02 = Pricing Procedure Y17J01 ）
  12. Set Calculation Schema-Purchasing(A13001)
  13. Define Schema Determination (Schema GrpPOrg 1310 + Sch.Grp Supp -> Calculation Schema A13001)
  14. Maintain Output Types(SPED)
  15. Maintain Output Determination Procedure (Output Determination Procedure V10000 -> Output Type SPED)
  16. Assign Output Determination Procedure(Delivery Type NCC3 -> Output Determination Procedure V10000 )
  17. Define Order Confirmations for Inbound Deliveries(Purchasing Document Category F + Order Type (Purchasing) ZNB2 + Plant 1310 + Storage Location 131C -> Confirmation Control Key 0004)
  18. Set Up Confirmation Control (Key 0004 -> Category LA )
  19. Define Internal Confirmation Categories (Confirmation Category LA -> Delivery Type EL + ELST)
  20. Define Item Category Determination in Deliveries(Delivery Type ELST + Item Category NORM + Usage V -> Item Category ELST)
  21. Define (Inbound) Delivery Item Categories(Item Category ELST -> Movement Type 109)
  22. Change Movement Type(Movement Type 685 -> GBB-VAY)
  23. Define Default Account Assignment(Activate PrfSeg for G/L Account corresponding to GBB-VAY)

 

Part B. Configuration Detail:

 

1 Define (Purchasing) Document Types

IMG Menu Path: SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Materials Management -> Purchasing -> Purchase Order -> Define Document Types for Purchase Orders

 

2 Define Shipping Data for Plants

IMG Menu Path: SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Materials Management -> Purchasing -> Purchase Order -> Set up Stock Transport Order -> Define Shipping Data for Plants

Parameters for Receiving Plant

Plant: Enter the receiving plant, in our case 1310.

Customer No Plant: Enter the customer code IC1310, which was previously created to represent the plant of company 1310.
*Note: Since company 1310 acts as the receiving/purchasing party (i.e., the customer of company 1710's plant) in this demo scenario, this field must not be left blank.

SlsOrg.Int.B (Sales Organization for Intercompany Billing): Leave blank or enter the sales organization of 1310.
*Note: Since company 1310 acts as the receiving/purchasing party instead of the supplying/selling party in this demo scenario, this field can be left blank in this context.

DistChannelIB (Distribution Channel for Intercompany Billing): Leave blank or enter the distribution channel of 1310.
*Note: Since company 1310 acts as the receiving/purchasing party instead of the supplying/selling party in this demo scenario, this field can be left blank in this context.

Div.Int.Billing (Division for Intercompany Billing): Leave blank or enter the division of 1310.
*Note: Since company 1310 acts as the receiving/purchasing party instead of the supplying/selling party in this demo scenario, this field can be left blank in this context.

Parameters for Supplying Plant

 Plant: Enter the supplying plant, in our case 1710.

Customer No Plant: Leave this blank or enter IC1710 (provided that the customer master record IC1710 has already been created).
*Note: Entering IC1710 here means that when plant 1710 procures goods from other affiliated plants within the group, IC1710 will serve as the Customer on the STO (specifically in the Customer field under the Shipping tab in the Item Details section). Since company 1710 acts as the supplying/selling plant (not the receiving/purchasing plant) in this demo scenario, leaving this field blank will not affect the process. However, if plant 1710 needs to function as a receiving party in an STO, you must enter the customer code representing plant 1710 (e.g., IC1710) here.

SlsOrg.Int.B (Sales Organization for Intercompany Billing): Enter the sales organization of 1710.
*Note: Because company 1710 acts as the supplying/selling party in this demo scenario, entering the sales organization of 1710 is mandatory in this context.

DistChannelIB (Distribution Channel for Intercompany Billing): Enter the distribution channel of 1710.
*Note: Because company 1710 acts as the supplying/selling party in this demo scenario, entering the distribution channel of 1710 is mandatory in this context.

Div.Int.Billing (Division for Intercompany Billing): Enter the division of 1710.
*Note: Because company 1710 acts as the supplying/selling party in this demo scenario, entering the division of 1710 is mandatory in this context.                 

 

3 Assign Document Type, One-Step Procedure, Underdelivery Tolerance

Supplying Plant 1710 +Receiving Plant 1310 -> STO Document Type ZNB2.

IMG Menu Path: SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Materials Management -> Purchasing -> Purchase Order -> Set up Stock Transport Order -> Assign Document Type, One-Step Procedure, Underdelivery Tolerance

Maintain a rule that links the supplying plant to the receiving plant and STO document Type.

SPlt: Enter the supplying plant, in our case 1710.

Plnt: Enter the receiving plant, in our case 1310.

Type: Select the purchasing document type. In our case, a custom document type ZNB1 is used.

One Step: This indicator determines whether the STO process uses a one-step or two-step procedure.

A: Checking this indicator means that goods issue and goods receipt are completed in a single action. When the supplying company 1710 posts goods issue (Tcode VL02N, Movement type 645) against the Outbound Delivery (created via tcode VL10B/VL10D), the system automatically and simultaneously posts the goods receipt (Movement type 101) for the receiving company 1310. Title of goods is transferred directly from the supplying plant (1710) to the receiving plant (1310) in one single step.

B: Deselect this indicator means a Two-step procedure): This is generally the more controlled approach. When the supplying company (1710) posts goods issue using movement type 681, unrestricted-use stock is transferred to special stock in transit (Special stock indicator T) rather than being immediately deducted from the supplying plant's stock. When ownership transfers to the purchasing company (1310) according to the agreed terms of contract between 2 parties, the supplying company executes VLPOD to reduce it's stock in transit and recognize COGS(movement type 685), both material document and accounting document would be generated. And simultaneously a goods receipt into valuated blocked stock(movement type 107) would be posted in the receiving company, both material document and accounting document would be created. Once the goods physically arrive, the receiving company posts goods receipt against the inbound delivery(movement type 109 ) to transfer valuated blocked stock to unrestricted stock, a material document would be generated but not accounting document. The two-step approach provides clearer accountability and better traceability, although it requires an additional step.

Underdeliv.tol.: Defines the permitted tolerance for partial delivery.

Based on my project experience, the "Two-Step Procedure" is recommended for cross-company code (intercompany) transactions to ensure clear financial accounting and rigorous inventory management. Although it requires an extra step in operations, it prevents a lot of future disputes and alignment issues.

 

4 Configure Delivery Type & Availability Check Procedure by Plant

STO Document Type(ZNB2) + Supplying Plant(1710) -> Delivery Type(NCC3) + Checking Rule(B).

IMG Menu Path: SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Materials Management -> Purchasing -> Purchase Order -> Set up Stock Transport Order -> Configure Delivery Type & Availability Check Procedure by Plant

Ty.：Enter the purchase document type defined for intercompany STO, such as ZNB2.

SPl: Enter the supplying plant,  in our example 1710

DlTy.：Select NCC3

CRl：Enter B

*This setting tells SAP to use the delivery process associated with delivery type NCC3 when an STO of type ZNB2 is created.

 

5 Define Item Category Determination in Deliveries

Delivery Type(NCC3) + Item Category Group(NORM from Material Master Data) + Usage(V is for STO) -> Item Category (NCC3)

IMG Menu Path: SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Logistics Execution -> Shipping -> Deliveries -> Define Item Category Determination in Deliveries

This Logistics Execution (LE) configuration determines the delivery item category automatically from delivery type NCC3, item category group NORM, and usage V.

 

6 Define Schedule Line Categories

Schedule Line Category(N3) -> Movement Type 681 & 685

IMG Menu Path: SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Sales and Distribution -> Sales -> Sales Documents -> Schedule Lines -> Define Schedule Line Categories.

When the supplying company (1710) posts goods issue in VL02N, movement type 681 transfers unrestricted-use stock to stock in transit (T stock). When the supplying company executes VLPOD, movement type 685 reduces stock in transit and recognizes the cost of goods sold (COGS).

 

7 Assign Schedule Line Categories

Item Category(NCC3) + MRP Type(Blank) -> Schedule Line Category(N3)

IMG Menu Path: SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Sales and Distribution -> Sales -> Sales Documents -> Schedule Lines -> Assign Schedule Line Categories

This setting make sure that Schedule Line Category N3 would be used when Item Category is NCC2(Which links to delivery type NCC3)

 

8 Maintain Copying Control for Billing Documents (Tgt IV, Source NCC3)

IMG Menu Path: SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Sales and Distribution -> Billing -> Billing Documents -> Maintain Copying Control for Billing Documents

If Price Source A is selected, the receiving/purchasing company’s STO condition value would be copied into the supplying company’s billing document as its billing condition. For example, the receiving/purchasing company's purchase price can be copied as the supplying company's intercompany sales price.

 

9 Define Condition Types PI01

IMG Menu Path: SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Materials Management -> Purchasing -> Conditions -> Define Price Determination Process -> Define Condition Types

Create 2 separate condition types to represent the sales price for the supplying company and the purchase price for the receiving company.

MM Condition type PI01（purchase price for the receiving company）

IMG Menu Path: SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Sales and Distribution -> Basic Functions -> Pricing -> Pricing Control -> Define Condition Types

SD Condition Type（sales price for the supplying company）

For the SD condition type, set Ref. Condition Type to the MM condition type with the same code, which is PI01, and set Ref. Application to M. Together with Price Source A in copying control, this allows the condition from the purchasing company's STO to be copied to the supplying company's billing document.

 

10 Setup Partner Determination for Deliveries

IMG Menu Path: SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Sales and Distribution -> Basic Functions -> Partner Determination -> Set Up Partner Determination Delivery Type -> Partner Determination Procedure

ZNIC is the account group used for customer IC1310. Assign partner determination procedure CUST to account group ZNIC.

 

11 Define and Assign (SD) Pricing Procedure Y17J01

IMG Menu Path: SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Sales and Distribution -> Basic Functions -> Pricing -> Pricing Control -> Define And Assign Pricing Procedures

The screenshot below shows only two of the condition types required for this procedure as an example.

 

12 Set Calculation Schema(MM Pricing Procedure)-Purchasing A13001

IMG Menu Path: SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Materials Management -> Purchasing -> Conditions -> Define Price Determination Process -> Set Calculation Schema - Purchasing

 

13 Define Schema（MM Pricing Procedure）Determination

IMG Menu Path: SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Materials Management -> Purchasing -> Conditions -> Define Price Determination Process -> Define Schema Group

IMG Menu Path: SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Materials Management -> Purchasing -> Conditions -> Define Price Determination Process -> Define Schema Determination

 

14 Maintain Output Types SPED

IMG Menu Path: SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Logistics Execution -> Shipping -> Basic Shipping Functions -> Output Control -> Output Determination -> Maintain Output Determination for Outbound Deliveries -> Maintain Output Types

Output type SPED enables SAP to create an inbound delivery automatically for the purchasing company (1310) when goods issue is posted with reference to outbound delivery for the supplying company's (1710).

 

15 Maintain Output Determination Procedure

Output Determination Procedure V10000 -> Output Type SPED

IMG Menu Path: SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Logistics Execution -> Shipping -> Basic Shipping Functions -> Output Control -> Output Determination -> Maintain Output Determination for Outbound Deliveries -> Maintain Output Determination Procedure

 

16 Assign Output Determination Procedure V10000

Delivery Type NCC3 -> Output Determination Procedure V10000

entry.title: Part 2 of 2 – Securing AI-Powered SAP Apps on SAP BTP: Single Sign-On and Role-Based Access with XSU
entry.content:
Overview

Part 1 of this series described how SAP S/4HANA data can be made available to AI clients through an MCP server running on SAP BTP. Once such data is exposed through a user interface, the application must meet the same security standards as any other access to SAP systems.

This article describes how a UI application on SAP BTP, Cloud Foundry runtime, authenticates users and enforces authorizations using two standard platform components:

  • Application router – the single entry point that handles user login and request forwarding.
  • SAP Authorization and Trust Management service (XSUAA) – the service that issues tokens and manages scopes, role templates and role collections.

The approach addresses three requirements:

  • Authentication: only users with a valid corporate identity can access the application.
  • Authorization: each user can access only the functions assigned to them.
  • Enforcement: authorization decisions are made on the server and cannot be bypassed in the browser.

Solution components

Component Responsibility

Identity provider (for example, SAP Cloud Identity Services connected to the corporate directory)Authenticates the user through corporate single sign-on.
XSUAAIssues a signed JSON Web Token (JWT) containing the user's scopes, based on the assigned role collections.
Application routerActs as the single public entry point. Redirects unauthenticated users to the login, maintains the user session and forwards requests to the application together with the token.
UI applicationValidates the token on every request and grants access only to the functions permitted by its scopes.

Users always access the application through the application router, and the application validates the token independently. This provides two separate layers of control.

Authentication flow

The following steps describe the first access of a user to the application:

  1. The browser requests the application through the application router. No session exists yet.
  2. The application router redirects the request to XSUAA, which delegates authentication to the configured identity provider.
  3. The user authenticates with the corporate login, typically through single sign-on.
  4. The identity provider confirms the user's identity to XSUAA. XSUAA determines the user's role collections and issues a JWT containing the corresponding scopes.
  5. The application router stores the token in its server-side session and returns the requested page. The browser receives only a session cookie.
  6. For each subsequent request, the application router attaches the token and forwards the request to the application.
  7. The application validates the token (signature, expiry and audience) and evaluates the scopes before processing the request.

 

Figure 1: Authentication flow. The highlighted arrows show where the token is transferred; it is exchanged only between server-side components.

When the session expires, the application router repeats the flow from step 2.

Authorization model

XSUAA separates the definition of permissions from their assignment through three levels:

Level Purpose Maintained by

ScopeA single permission that the application checksDeveloper, in xs-security.json
Role templateGroups one or more scopes into a functional roleDeveloper, in xs-security.json
Role collectionBundles roles for assignment to users or user groupsAdministrator, in the SAP BTP cockpit

The complete xs-security.json is shown in step 1 of the configuration below.

With this model, access is managed entirely in the SAP BTP cockpit. Granting or revoking access requires no code change and no redeployment. Assigning role collections to user groups from the identity provider, rather than to individual users, keeps access aligned with organizational changes automatically.

Configuration steps

The following examples use generic names (my-xsuaa, my-approuter, my-ui-app) and placeholders in angle brackets. Replace them with the values of your own subaccount.

Step 1: Define the security descriptor (xs-security.json)

{
  "xsappname": "my-ui-app",
  "tenant-mode": "dedicated",
  "scopes": [
    { "name": "$XSAPPNAME.Display", "description": "Use the application" },
    { "name": "$XSAPPNAME.Monitor", "description": "Use the monitoring functions" }
  ],
  "role-templates": [
    { "name": "Viewer",         "scope-references": ["$XSAPPNAME.Display"] },
    { "name": "MonitoringUser", "scope-references": ["$XSAPPNAME.Display", "$XSAPPNAME.Monitor"] }
  ],
  "role-collections": [
    { "name": "App Viewers",      "role-template-references": ["$XSAPPNAME.Viewer"] },
    { "name": "Monitoring Users", "role-template-references": ["$XSAPPNAME.MonitoringUser"] }
  ],
  "oauth2-configuration": {
    "redirect-uris": ["https://<approuter-host>.cfapps.<region>.hana.ondemand.com/**"]
  }
}

Create the XSUAA service instance from this file. Later changes are applied to the same instance with update-service:

cf create-service xsuaa application my-xsuaa -c xs-security.json
cf update-service my-xsuaa -c xs-security.json

Step 2: Configure the application router

The application router is a small Node.js application based on the @SAP/approuter package. It needs three files.

package.json:

{
  "name": "my-approuter",
  "dependencies": { "@sap/approuter": "^20" },
  "scripts": { "start": "node node_modules/@sap/approuter/approuter.js" }
}

xs-app.json – every route requires an XSUAA login, and requests are forwarded to the UI application:

{
  "welcomeFile": "/",
  "authenticationMethod": "route",
  "logout": { "logoutEndpoint": "/logout" },
  "routes": [
    {
      "source": "^/(.*)$",
      "target": "/$1",
      "destination": "ui-app",
      "authenticationType": "xsuaa",
      "csrfProtection": false
    }
  ]
}

manifest.yml – the destination ui-app points to the UI application, and forwardAuthToken passes the user's token on:

applications:
  - name: my-approuter
    memory: 256M
    services:
      - my-xsuaa
    env:
      destinations: >
        [ { "name": "ui-app",
            "url": "https://<ui-app-host>.cfapps.<region>.hana.ondemand.com",
            "forwardAuthToken": true } ]

Set csrfProtection according to your application. If the UI application implements its own CSRF protection, the router's protection can be switched off for its routes, as shown above.

Step 3: Bind XSUAA to the UI application

The UI application needs the same XSUAA instance to validate the tokens it receives. Add it to the application's manifest.yml:

applications:
  - name: my-ui-app
    services:
      - my-xsuaa

Deploy both applications:

cf push my-ui-app
cf push my-approuter

Step 4: Configure trust and assign roles

In the SAP BTP cockpit, open Security → Trust Configuration and establish trust with your identity provider. Then assign the role collections under Security → Role Collections, preferably to user groups. With the SAP BTP command line interface, the assignment can also be scripted:

btp assign security/role-collection "Monitoring Users" --to-user <user@example.com>

Server-side authorization checks

The application router ensures that only authenticated users reach the application. Fine-grained authorization is performed by the application itself, on the server, for every request:

  1. Validate the forwarded token and reject requests with a missing, expired or foreign token.
  2. Read the scopes from the token.
  3. Expose only the functions and data permitted by those scopes, both in the user interface and in the server's API responses.

Because these checks run on the server, they cannot be circumvented by modifying the page or by calling the application's API directly.

For Node.js applications, SAP provides the @SAP/xssec and @SAP/xsenv packages for token validation. A minimal example with Express:

const express = require("express");
const xsenv = require("@sap/xsenv");
const { XsuaaService, createSecurityContext } = require("@sap/xssec");

const xsuaa = new XsuaaService(xsenv.getServices({ xsuaa: { tag: "xsuaa" } }).xsuaa);
const app = express();

// 1. Validate the token on every request
app.use(async (req, res, next) => {
  try {
    req.authInfo = await createSecurityContext(xsuaa, { req });
    next();
  } catch (e) {
    res.status(401).json({ error: "Not authenticated" });
  }
});

// 2. Require a scope for a protected function
const requireScope = (scope) => (req, res, next) =>
  req.authInfo.checkLocalScope(scope) ? next() : res.status(403).json({ error: "Not authorized" });

app.get("/api/monitoring", requireScope("Monitor"), (req, res) => {
  res.json({ status: "ok" });   // only reached with the Monitor scope
});

app.listen(process.env.PORT || 8080);

For Java applications, the SAP Cloud Security Services Integration Library (java-security) offers the same functions.

Backend connectivity

User authentication protects access to the application. Communication between the application and SAP S/4HANA is a separate, technical connection through an SAP BTP destination and the SAP Cloud Connector, using a technical user. As a result, SAP S/4HANA authorizes the technical user rather than the individual end user.

This is suitable for a proof of concept. For productive use, principal propagation should be considered, so that the end user's own SAP authorizations are also applied in the backend system.

Handling session expiry in the UI

When the application router session expires, background requests (for example fetch calls) receive a login redirect or an HTTP 401 instead of data. A reload of the page lets the application router restart the authentication flow:

async function callApi(url, options) {
  const res = await fetch(url, { credentials: "include", ...options });
  const isJson = (res.headers.get("content-type") || "").includes("application/json");
  if (res.status === 401 || !isJson) {
    window.location.reload();        // the application router redirects to the login
    return null;
  }
  return res.json();
}

Key considerations

Topic Consideration

Role changesScopes are written into the token at login. After a role collection is assigned or removed, the user must log in again for the change to take effect.
Session expiryBackground requests cannot complete an interactive login. When a session expires, the application should reload the page so that the application router can restart the authentication flow.
Service updatesUpdates to the XSUAA instance must be applied with the intended xs-security.json. Verify the resulting roles in the SAP BTP cockpit after each update.
Client-side restrictionsHiding functions in the user interface does not replace server-side authorization checks.
CredentialsTechnical credentials, such as API keys, should be provided through service bindings rather than environment variables or source code.

Summary

The application router and XSUAA provide a UI application on SAP BTP with the same authentication and authorization model as any other SAP BTP application:

  • A single entry point with corporate single sign-on.
  • Permissions carried in a signed token, defined by developers and assigned by administrators.
  • Authorization decisions enforced on the server.

An application that exposes SAP data through AI therefore requires no dedicated security model; it integrates into the standard security concept of SAP BTP. Principal propagation is the logical next step to extend user-specific authorizations to the SAP backend.

entry.title: EWM Outbound: The Correct Sequence for Correcting a Delivery Item After Warehouse Task Confirmation
entry.content:
Introduction
One of the most common process mistakes in SAP Extended Warehouse Management (EWM) outbound operations happens when a warehouse coordinator or logistics analyst needs to correct a delivery item,  a quantity change, a batch reassignment, or a batch split sub-item removal after the warehouse task has already been confirmed and the stock is packed into a Handling Unit (HU).

The instinct is to go directly to the ERP delivery (VL02N) and make the correction. It seems logical: the issue is in the delivery document, so fix the delivery document. However, this approach, while intuitive, breaks the reference link between the EWM HU and the ERP delivery item, causing a silent but severe data inconsistency that only surfaces when the system tries to proceed to the next step in the outbound process.

This post documents the problem pattern, explains why it happens, and provides the correct step-by-step sequence to follow whenever a delivery item correction is needed after picking has been confirmed.

The Problem — What Goes Wrong

Symptoms

When the wrong sequence is followed, the following symptoms appear in EWM:

  • Warehouse request is empty — no items available to generate new warehouse tasks
  • Physical stock in the HU shows Item = 0 — the HU contains stock but references a delivery item that no longer exists
  • Subsequent warehouse task cannot be created — the outbound flow to staging or GI zone is blocked
  • Goods Issue cannot be posted — the entire outbound billing chain is halted

The Root Cause

In SAP EWM, when a warehouse task is confirmed, the system creates a direct link between the physical stock in the Handling Unit and the delivery item in the EWM Outbound Delivery Order (ODO). This link is stored at the HU item level with a reference to the specific delivery item number.

When the delivery item is then modified or deleted in ERP — for example, by removing a Batch Split (BSP) sub-item or zeroing out the main item quantity — EWM is not aware of this change until a full redistribution of the delivery occurs. In the meantime, the HU item still holds the old reference. If that delivery item no longer exists, the reference becomes orphaned, and the field Item in the HU physical stock view shows 0 (zero), meaning: "this stock is assigned to this delivery, but to an item that no longer exists."

The result:

HU has stock → delivery item reference = 0 (orphaned)
Warehouse request → empty (no valid items to pick)
Next step (YEST / GI zone) → cannot be triggered
Goods Issue → blocked

How to Identify the Issue

Before attempting any correction, confirm the inconsistency:

Step 1 — Check the Warehouse Request

  • Run the warehouse task creation transaction for the affected ODO
  • If the "Solic. depósito" (Warehouse Request) tab is empty → issue confirmed

Step 2 — Check Physical Stock (/SCWM/ADHU)

  1. Run /SCWM/ADHU
  2. Search by Warehouse Number and Document (ODO number)
  3. Open the Physical Stock (Estoque físico) tab
  4. Look for entries where Item = 0 → orphaned HU item confirmed

Step 3 — Trace the Sequence (/SCWM/ACTLOG)

  1. Run /SCWM/ACTLOG
  2. Filter by Warehouse Number and ODO number
  3. Look for a delivery modification that occurred after a warehouse task confirmation
  4. This confirms the wrong sequence was followed

The Wrong Sequence ❌

1. WT confirmed (picking done, stock in HU)     ✓
2. Delivery modified in ERP (VL02N)             ← WRONG — HU not unpacked first
3. Item deleted / quantity zeroed out           ← HU now references non-existing item
4. Item = 0 appears in HU physical stock        ← Inconsistency created
5. Subsequent WT creation fails                 ← Process blocked

The Correct Sequence ✅

Whenever a delivery item needs to be corrected after a warehouse task has been confirmed and stock is packed in an HU, always follow this sequence:

Step 1 — Cancel / Reverse the Warehouse Task Confirmation

  • Navigate to the confirmed warehouse task in EWM
  • Reverse/cancel the confirmation to return stock to its source bin
  • The HU assignment is released

Step 2 — Unpack / Deassign the HU Item

  1. Run /SCWM/ADHU
  2. Locate the HU containing the stock for the affected item
  3. Remove (deassign) the item from the HU
  4. Confirm the physical stock no longer shows the delivery item reference

Step 3 — Perform the Delivery Correction in ERP

  • Run VL02N in ERP
  • Apply the necessary correction (delete BSP sub-item, change batch, adjust quantity, etc.)
  • Save the delivery

Step 4 — Re-distribute the Delivery to EWM

  • Re-save the delivery or use VL06O to push the updated delivery to EWM
  • Confirm the ODO in EWM reflects the corrected items

Step 5 — Re-generate and Execute the Warehouse Task

  • Create a new warehouse task for the corrected items
  • Confirm the task via /SCWM/RFUI or the appropriate RF transaction
  • Pack stock into the HU again
  • Continue the outbound flow normally

Visual Summary

✅ CORRECT SEQUENCE

WT Confirmed → Stock in HU
        ↓
[1] Reverse WT confirmation
        ↓
[2] Unpack HU item (/SCWM/ADHU)
        ↓
[3] Modify delivery in ERP (VL02N)
        ↓
[4] Re-distribute to EWM (VL06O)
        ↓
[5] Re-generate WT → confirm → pack → continue flow

Why This Matters — Business Impact

Skipping steps 1 and 2 before modifying the delivery may seem like a time-saving shortcut, but the consequences are severe:

Impact Area Consequence
Warehouse OperationsPicking tasks cannot be created — pickers are blocked
Outbound LogisticsGoods Issue cannot be posted
Customer BillingInvoice generation delayed or blocked
Data IntegrityOrphaned HU items require manual correction by support team
System RecoveryEach affected ODO requires individual manual data fix

In large warehouse environments with high-volume outbound processing, a single incorrect sequence applied to multiple deliveries can result in significant operational disruption and financial exposure.

Prevention — Process and Authorization Controls

Process Training

Warehouse supervisors and logistics coordinators should be trained on this sequence. A simple rule to communicate to the team:

"Never modify a delivery in ERP if the stock has already been confirmed and packed in EWM. Always unpack and reverse first."

Authorization Control (Recommended)

Consider restricting the user role authorization in ERP to prevent deletion or modification of delivery items that have active HU assignments in EWM. This removes the possibility of the wrong sequence being followed unintentionally.

Proactive Monitoring

Implement a daily check in /SCWM/MON for ODOs that:

  • Have HUs assigned
  • Have no open warehouse tasks
  • Have not yet posted Goods Issue

Catching these early (before the shipping window) avoids escalation to a business-down situation. Moreover, this proactive monitoring should be performed only when the behavior is already noticed but not fixed or identified how many deliveries could be affected by this behavior. 

Conclusion

The EWM outbound process enforces a tight coupling between delivery items in ERP and physical stock in Handling Units. This design ensures data consistency but requires discipline when corrections are needed mid-process. The correct sequence — reverse → unpack → correct → redistribute → re-execute — must always be followed when modifying a delivery item after warehouse task confirmation.

Understanding this sequence is fundamental for anyone operating or supporting EWM outbound processing, and implementing the appropriate process controls prevents it from becoming a recurring incident.

 Author: Jacson Folmer Dias — EWM Consultant | SAP Global Delivery Hub Americas LAC

entry.title: Step Zero Before You Put AI on an SAP S/4HANA Process
entry.content:
The person who always closes the purchasing process goes on vacation. Their replacement has the manual, the user ID and access to S/4HANA. By mid-morning, they have already asked five times how to move forward. None of the answers were in the manual.

Now swap the replacement for a Joule agent or an automated workflow. It won’t ask five times. It will do exactly what the documentation says.

 

 

 

That is the question worth asking before you put AI or automation on a process in SAP S/4HANA: is the process written down, or is it held up by the people who know how to run it?

Today there are three good guides for governing AI in business processes: COSO’s guidance on generative AI, FEI’s framework on internal control over financial reporting, and SAP’s playbook for ERP automation. All three agree on the fundamentals: AI in a process needs controls, and those controls must be testable. SAP’s playbook even asks teams to map decision points and codify business rules. What none of them offers is a way to check whether the process is actually written down, or held up by people.

If it isn’t, something happens that nobody sees: the automation passes its tests, because the tests have the same gap as the documentation.

These four tests help you find out first. Each one runs on what is already in S/4HANA, with no new tools and no budget.

1. The replacement test

Give the process documentation to someone who doesn’t run the process, and ask them to run it end to end in the test system, using only what is written.

Threshold: if they need to ask more than three times, the process is not described. It is held up by a person.

It is the most uncomfortable test and the fastest: half a day. And it leaves no room for interpretation: either the purchase order reaches the invoice with what is written, or it doesn’t.

2. The exception test

Take one month of purchase orders and journal entries, and count how many were resolved outside the normal path. S/4HANA keeps a trail:

  • Purchase orders changed after release: every change is stored in change documents (tables CDHDR and CDPOS, object class EINKBELEG).
  • Purchase orders without a prior requisition or outside a contract, when the procedure says otherwise: on the PO item, the requisition field (EKPO-BANFN) and the contract field (EKPO-KONNR) are empty.
  • Manual journal entries at month-end: filter them by document type (SA in the standard) and separate them from the ones the system posts on its own.

Threshold: if more than one in ten needed a decision that is not in the procedure, the process runs on unwritten judgment.

One clarification: recurring manual entries that are on the closing checklist don’t count. The ones that count are those nobody could explain with the procedure in hand.

Every “it depends” is a rule that exists and was never written down. “If the supplier is new, I ask for approval even when the amount doesn’t require it.” An agent doesn’t know that rule.

Time: one day.

3. The repeated-question test

For one week, log every question to the help desk or to key users about this process, and the transaction or Fiori app where it came up.

Threshold: if the same question shows up twice, the documentation describes something different from what is actually done.

This test doesn’t measure people. It measures the distance between the document and the operation.

Time: one week, alongside normal work.

4. The control test

List the controls in the process and ask, for each one, where it lives:

  • Configured in S/4HANA (automated control): a release strategy or approval workflow, a required field, data the system won’t let you save if it’s missing.
  • Or in a person (manual control): someone who reviews a report and “notices.”

Threshold: if the control depends on someone looking at a report, it won’t survive automation.

Configured controls scale on their own, as long as nobody turns them off or works around them. Controls that depend on a person noticing something odd stop existing when volume goes up and nobody is looking.

Time: one day with the process owner.

What to do with the result

None of the four is a pass or fail for the whole process. What they give you is a map: which part of the process is defined, and which part is held up by people who know.

The defined part is ready to automate in S/4HANA. The rest has to be written down first, and the team bringing the tool can’t do that work. It’s done by the people who know the process.

The thresholds are a starting point, not a standard. Adjust them to the risk: a financial close deserves a stricter bar than an office supplies purchase.

Why it matters more than it seems

FEI’s framework lists performance testing among its control approaches: comparing what the AI produces against what is considered correct. It is the most rigorous approach. And “correct” is built from how the process runs today.

If part of that “how” was never written down, the reference is incomplete from day one. The automation passes the test, because the test has the same gap as the documentation. Nothing fails, no alert goes off, and the lost judgment doesn’t show up on any S/4HANA dashboard.

What this does not mean

It doesn’t mean documenting everything before automating anything. That would be the perfect excuse to never start.

It means the process description stops being one more project deliverable and becomes part of the control system. It changes category and it changes owner: it no longer belongs to the project team. It belongs to the process owner.

 

If you have run any of these tests on a real process in S/4HANA, tell me which one your process failed. In my experience, the second one surprises people the most.

References

  • COSO, Achieving Effective Internal Control Over Generative AI (February 2026).
  • FEI, Committee on Corporate Reporting, AI Framework: Internal Control Over Financial Reporting (June 2026).
  • SAP, ERP Automation at Scale: A Playbook for AI-Enabled Operations (SAP blog).

entry.title: Beyond Architecture: Through My Lens on the Multidimensional Architect in the Age of AI
entry.content:
The Beginning – 2024: Rethinking the Role of an Enterprise Architect

My journey with the SAP Multidimensional Architect Program began in 2024, when I had the opportunity to attend its inaugural program. What made the experience particularly impactful was that it challenged my traditional understanding of Enterprise Architecture and broadened my perspective on what it truly takes to become an effective Enterprise Architect.

Building on the foundation established in 2024, the 2025 edition of the SAP Multidimensional Architect Program took the Enterprise Architect journey a step further. While the first year challenged us to rethink the role of an architect and develop the right mindset, 2025 focused on expanding our capabilities and becoming truly multidimensional  bringing together technology expertise, business acumen, strategic thinking, leadership, and the ability to influence people and organizations.

First cohort of EA-2024

 

2025 – Becoming a Multidimensional Architect: Beyond Technology, Towards Business Impact

The SAP Multidimensional Architect Program 2025 was a transformative five-day journey that brought together technology, business strategy, AI, leadership, and human connections. It challenged traditional perceptions of Enterprise Architecture and reinforced that the future architect must be more than a technology expert  someone who can connect business vision with technology execution, embrace AI-driven innovation, influence organizational change, and inspire people through collaboration and purpose.

One of the strongest messages was that architecture must start with business outcomes, not technology choices. Architects need to understand the business context, recognize organizational challenges, translate strategic objectives into technology-enabled capabilities, and help decision-makers see the value of the transformation journey. It is not enough to recommend a solution; we must be able to explain why it matters, what value it creates, and how it moves the organization closer to its long-term vision.

The program also reinforced several dimensions that define the modern Enterprise Architect:

  • Business and strategic thinking: Move beyond solution design to understand business priorities, operating models, value drivers, and the broader transformation agenda.

  • AI and emerging technologies: Develop the curiosity and understanding to explore AI-driven innovation, assess its potential, and identify meaningful opportunities to create business value.

  • Leadership and influence: Architecture is increasingly about influencing decisions, aligning stakeholders, navigating complexity, and bringing people together around a shared vision even without direct authority.

  • Communication and storytelling: A compelling architecture vision needs a compelling story. Architects must simplify complexity, communicate with different audiences, articulate the value of change, and build confidence in the roadmap.

  • Human-centered architecture: Technology transformation is ultimately about people. Empathy, active listening, collaboration, trust, and the ability to inspire change are as important as technical depth.

  • Collaboration and community: Learning from peers, exchanging experiences, challenging assumptions, and building professional relationships strengthen the collective capabilities of the Enterprise Architecture community.

Perhaps the biggest takeaway was that Enterprise Architecture is not just about designing systems, frameworks, or roadmaps; it is about building capabilities, enabling decisions, connecting people, and creating sustainable business outcomes. The program concluded not simply with the completion of five days of learning, but with the beginning of a stronger, more connected, and collaborative Enterprise Architect community.

My reflections and personal takeaways

For me, the 2025 program reinforced an important shift in how I approach my own professional journey: moving from being a technology leader who delivers complex transformations to becoming an architect who shapes transformation strategy and business outcomes.

With more than two decades of experience in the SAP ecosystem, working across large-scale transformations, S/4HANA conversions via Downtime Optimized Conversion (DoC) , Zero Downtime Option (ZDO), and complex customer landscapes, I have seen firsthand that technical excellence is essential  but it is only one part of the equation. The ability to connect technology decisions with business priorities, communicate the bigger picture, influence stakeholders, and lead people through change is what creates lasting impact.

The overall program experience and listening to all the intellectual leaders inspired me to look beyond the technical boundaries of Enterprise Architecture and reflect on how knowledge, experience, and practical insights can be transformed into something meaningful for the wider SAP community. It motivated me to bring together my years of hands-on experience in S/4HANA transformations and Zero Downtime Option (ZDO) into my book, “Mastering S/4HANA Upgrades and Updates via ZDO – Zero Downtime Optimization.” Writing this book became an opportunity to share practical learnings, address real-world upgrade and downtime challenges, and help fellow architects and SAP professionals navigate complex transformation journeys with greater confidence.

If 2024 was about changing the architect's mindset, 2025 was about expanding those dimensions  and turning experience into knowledge that can inspire and empower others. The program reinforced that architects should not only design and deliver transformation but also contribute to the community, share their expertise, and create lasting value beyond individual projects. It also set the stage for the next evolution in 2026: How do we architect for an AI-driven and increasingly autonomous enterprise?

Second Cohort of EA - 2025

 

 

2026 – Architecting the Autonomous Enterprise: The Enterprise Architect in the Age of AI

If 2024 was about changing the architect's mindset and 2025 was about expanding the architect's dimensions, 2026 brought us to the next frontier: redefining Enterprise Architecture in the age of AI and the Autonomous Enterprise.

The 2026 SAP Multidimensional Architect Program, hosted at the SAP Institute for Product and Engineering in San Ramon, brought together more than 100 architects for another immersive learning experience. The conversations moved beyond understanding emerging technologies to exploring how AI, agentic capabilities, trusted enterprise data, strategic leadership, and human intelligence will shape the future of organizations  and, more importantly, the future role of Enterprise Architects.

What stood out was the shift from discussing what AI can do to understanding how architects can help organizations adopt it responsibly, connect it to business priorities, and translate its potential into measurable outcomes.

The Future-Ready Architect: Learn, Unlearn and Relearn

The initial program sessions set the tone by exploring the Future-Ready Architect, the Autonomous Enterprise, AI-enabled productivity, and the human skills required to navigate continuous change.

One of the strongest messages was the importance of moving from IQ to EQ to LQ – Learning Quotient. In a world where technology and AI capabilities are evolving rapidly, technical knowledge alone is not enough. Our ability to remain curious, challenge assumptions, adapt, and continuously learn will determine how effectively we lead through change.

Some important takeaways are - 

  • Learn, unlearn and relearn: Be willing to challenge established practices and continuously evolve our thinking.

  • Balance technology with human intelligence: Combine technical expertise with emotional intelligence, empathy, and sound human judgment.

  • Connect architecture to business outcomes: Ensure technology and AI initiatives solve meaningful business problems.

  • Practice the art of subtraction: Simplify complexity, eliminate unnecessary work, and create space to focus on what truly matters.

  • Build responsible AI strategies: Treat governance, accountability, and trust as essential elements of AI adoption.

The message was clear: the future-ready architect is not necessarily the person who knows the most technologies, but the one who can adapt, ask better questions, and bring the right people and capabilities together.

 From Technology Advisor to Strategic Business Leader

Program moved with more deep dive focus sessions into how AI is changing the enterprise and the role architects must play in shaping that change. The discussions connected the Autonomous Enterprise, industry AI, trusted data and context with the evolving strategic responsibilities of Enterprise Architecture.

A particularly powerful metaphor was “The Empty Chair at the Strategic Table by Dr. Michael R. Blaschke

Enterprise Architecture needs a seat at the table where business strategy and AI investment decisions are made. But that seat cannot simply be claimed because of an architect's title or technical experience. It must be earned through meaningful business relationships, the quality of questions we ask, the perspectives we bring, and the value we create.

Some of the Key takeaways included:

  • Start with WHY before HOW: Understand the business problem and desired outcome before recommending a technology solution.

  • Think and communicate like an executive: Connect architecture decisions to business priorities, value, and long-term direction.

  • Design for enterprise capabilities: Look beyond individual applications and solutions to the capabilities the organization needs to build.

  • Build relationships across the business: Engage business leaders and C-suite stakeholders early rather than waiting for technology decisions to be made.

  • Exercise judgment in AI adoption: Understand where AI can create meaningful value — and recognize when a different approach may be more appropriate.

One thought from the day particularly resonated: “We don't just move data; we move human possibilities.” It was a reminder that architecture is ultimately about enabling people, improving decisions, and creating opportunities through technology.

Meeting the mastermind behind Business Architecture and the author of Strategy to Reality - Whynde Kuehn in person was another defining highlight of this journey. The interaction helped me gain a deeper understanding of how businesses operate, how strategy translates into execution, and how architecture can bridge the gap between business vision and technology delivery. It reinforced an important perspective in my professional evolution: the transition from a Technology Architect to a Business Architect, and ultimately to an Enterprise Architect, requires a fundamental shift in thinking — from designing technology solutions to understanding business capabilities, shaping strategy, and enabling enterprise-wide transformation.

 

From AI Possibilities to Agentic AI Value Realization

Program moved the conversation from the promise of AI to the practical realities of Agentic AI. The focus was on trusted enterprise context, realizing business value from AI agents, and maintaining human responsibility as organizations move toward greater autonomy.

Some of the survey findings highlighted a significant gap between AI experimentation and enterprise-wide value realization. Organizations may be exploring AI agents, but scaling them requires much more than technology implementation. It requires clear business objectives, trusted data, enterprise context, governance, accountability, and measurable outcomes.

Another finding was equally important: only 9% of respondents said Enterprise Architecture leads AI decisions in their organizations, while 40% indicated that EA is informed after decisions have been made or is not involved but is still expected to deliver.

This reinforces the importance of Enterprise Architects becoming active participants in AI strategy and investment decisions — not simply implementation partners brought in after the direction has already been established.

Some of the key takeaways from the sessions were:

  • Define business value upfront: Every AI initiative should have a clear purpose and measurable business KPIs.

  • Build trusted enterprise context: AI agents need reliable data, business context, and organizational knowledge to deliver meaningful results.

  • Bring Enterprise Architecture into AI decisions early: Architects should help shape the strategy, operating model, integration, and governance of AI initiatives.

  • Measure the work AI creates, not just the work it saves: Evaluate the broader impact of AI on business processes, productivity, and new opportunities.

  • Keep human judgment and accountability central: As autonomy increases, responsible oversight and decision-making become even more important.

  • Explore practical AI opportunities for architects: Documentation, design, discovery, and other architecture activities can benefit from AI-enabled productivity.

 

My Reflections – From Architecting Technology to Shaping the AI-Driven Enterprise

Having participated in the Multidimensional Architect Program since its inception in 2024, I see a clear progression in both the program and the expectations placed on Enterprise Architects.

The 2026 discussions made me reflect on how our profession is evolving. For years, architects have focused on designing technology landscapes, defining integration strategies, establishing governance, and delivering complex transformation programs. Those responsibilities remain important, but the emergence of AI and autonomous agents is expanding the scope of our contribution.

The architect of tomorrow must be able to connect business strategy, enterprise architecture, trusted data, AI capabilities, and human judgment. We need to understand not only how AI works, but where it creates value, how it fits into the enterprise operating model, how it can be governed responsibly, and how its outcomes can be measured.

For me, the biggest shift is this: we must move from architecting solutions for the business to helping the business reimagine what is possible with AI.

This also connects closely with my own professional journey — from leading complex SAP transformations and S/4HANA upgrade programs to exploring AI-driven architecture, automation, and intelligent operations. The program further strengthened my interest in applying AI not just as another technology layer, but as an enabler of better decisions, more efficient operations, and new business capabilities.

Three Years of Evolution – One Changing Profession

Looking back at the three editions, I see more than the evolution of a learning program. I see a reflection of how the Enterprise Architect role itself is changing.

Year       Focus                                                                     The shift

2024Rethinking the ArchitectFrom technology expertise to a broader mindset
2025Becoming MultidimensionalFrom technical leadership to business, people, and strategic influence
2026Architecting the Autonomous EnterpriseFrom AI awareness to AI strategy, agentic capabilities, and measurable business value

Each year built on the previous one. The journey started with transforming how we think, expanded into how we lead and influence, and now challenges us to shape the future of AI-driven enterprises.

The Road Ahead – What Will Define the Enterprise Architect of Tomorrow?

As AI continues to evolve, I believe the Enterprise Architect will increasingly become a bridge between business strategy, technology innovation, and human potential.

The architects who will make the greatest impact are those who can:

  • Think strategically and understand business value.

  • Combine deep technology expertise with AI fluency.

  • Design enterprise-wide capabilities rather than isolated solutions.

  • Translate complexity into clear stories and actionable roadmaps.

  • Champion trusted, responsible, and governed AI adoption.

  • Influence decisions, inspire people, and lead organizational change.

  • Continuously learn, unlearn, relearn, and share knowledge with the community.

My journey through the SAP Multidimensional Architect Program over these three years has been both inspiring and motivating. It has encouraged me to challenge my own perspectives, broaden my professional horizons, share my experiences through writing, and continuously explore how emerging technologies can create meaningful impact.

I am grateful to the SAP Institute for Product and Engineering, the program organizers, speakers, fellow architects, and the wider Enterprise Architecture community for creating an environment where learning goes beyond presentations — through conversations, shared experiences, new perspectives, and lasting connections.

 

Personal Achievements & Highlights – When Learning Turned into a Proud Moment

Beyond the incredible learning, insights, and inspiration I gained throughout the three-day journey, the most memorable moment was saved for the very end truly the icing on the cake!

A special and heartfelt appreciation to Paul Kurchina for taking the opportunity to recognize and promote my book, “SAP S/4HANA Upgrades & Updates: Mastering Zero Downtime Option,” and for sharing its relevance with the architect community. Seeing my work acknowledged and highlighted in such a forum was both humbling and immensely rewarding. It was particularly meaningful because the book represents years of hands-on experience, practical learnings, and a personal commitment to sharing knowledge with the broader SAP ecosystem.

What made the moment even more special was the connection highlighted between the book's subject and the value our SAP MaxAttention team can bring to customers through our expertise in Zero Downtime Option (ZDO) and SAP S/4HANA upgrade approaches, we can help customers address one of their biggest transformation concerns minimizing business downtime while navigating complex upgrades and conversions. It was a great opportunity to reinforce how our team's experience, guidance, and technical capabilities can help customers plan and execute their transformation journeys with reduced downtime and greater confidence.

For me, this was more than just a book promotion. It was a proud moment where personal knowledge-sharing, professional achievement, and customer value came together. It reinforced my belief that the experience we gain through customer engagements becomes even more meaningful when we document it, share it, and use it to help others succeed.

I couldn't have asked for a more fulfilling way to conclude this year's program — taking away new perspectives, strengthening connections, and seeing my own contribution create visibility and potential value for the wider SAP community.

One of the most influential aspects of this three-year journey has been the opportunity to learn from Ferose V R, SVP and Head of SAP Institute for Product and Engineering, San Ramon. His distinctive style of communication, ability to simplify complex ideas, powerful storytelling, and thoughtful way of connecting technology with people and purpose have been a constant source of inspiration throughout my professional journey.

Beyond the knowledge he shares, his approach to writing, articulating ideas, and communicating with clarity and conviction has encouraged me to become a better storyteller, strengthen my own communication skills, and share my experiences and learnings with a wider professional community.

 

My biggest takeaway from these three years is simple:

  • 2024 taught us to think differently. 2025 inspired us to become multidimensional. 2026 challenged us to architect and think differently in AI world.
  • The future Enterprise Architect will not simply design the enterprise of today. They will help shape the autonomous, intelligent, and human-centered enterprise of tomorrow.

And that, to me, is the true meaning of being a Multidimensional Architect and i will try to follow and implement this pledge as i continue to follow the Enterprise Architecture practice
